subtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MAKE SOURCES OF INFORMATION OF PRESS AND RADIO CONFIDENTIAL

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Sfuari S. Garson (Minisler of Jusiice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CANADA EVIDENCE ACT
subtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MAKE SOURCES OF INFORMATION OF PRESS AND RADIO CONFIDENTIAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Howe) has asked me to reply to a question which was directed to him yesterday by the hon. member for Prince Albert. The question was:
Will the government give consideration to introducing an amendment to the Canada Evidence Act at the present session so that the sources of information of press and radio in any future action shall be considered confidential and inadmissible as evidence?
This question arises, as the hon. member has indicated, as a result of a certain action

in the British Columbia courts entitled Wismer v. Maclean-Hunter Publishing Company and Fraser. This was a civil action for damages arising out of an alleged libel. I understand that in the course of these proceedings it was held that where malice is a relevant issue the defendant may be asked the name of his informant unless it appears that the plaintiff had an improper motive in seeking that information.
The Canada Evidence Act does not apply in the case of civil actions in the provincial courts; consequently the amendment to the Canada Evidence Act which has been suggested by the hon. member for Prince Albert would be entirely ineffective in any such future action.

maintopic: CANADA EVIDENCE ACT
subtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MAKE SOURCES OF INFORMATION OF PRESS AND RADIO CONFIDENTIAL
speechtext: Would the Minister of Justice comment on the fact that in the Alberta press case of 1938 the Supreme Court of Canada held that freedom of the press was not a matter of provincial jurisdiction but came within the ambit of the federal authority as part of our parliamentary system.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CANADA EVIDENCE ACT
subtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MAKE SOURCES OF INFORMATION OF PRESS AND RADIO CONFIDENTIAL
speechtext: I should be glad to comment upon that. My hon. friend is quite right in what he says about the Alberta press case. But that point has nothing to do with the judgment in the present case under discussion which was in a civil action for damages for an alleged libel; and the question we are discussing was as to whether a defendant could by interrogatories be asked the source of his information. I am sure that my hon. friend will agree that if it were thought desirable, as he seems to think it is, that an amendment to an evidence act should be passed to apply to a situation of that kind, it would have to be to the British Columbia evidence act and not to the Canada Evidence Act.

maintopic: CANADA EVIDENCE ACT
subtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MAKE SOURCES OF INFORMATION OF PRESS AND RADIO CONFIDENTIAL
speechtext: I was just wondering whether in view of the supreme court decision that would be so.

maintopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT
NATIONAL HOUSING ACT
subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.

speechtext:
The house in committee on Bill No. 102, to promote the construction of new houses, the repair and modernization of existing houses, and the improvement of housing and building conditions-Mr. Winters-Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
On clause 1-Short title.

maintopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT
subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with the return to the House of Commons of Bill No. 102, the house is again faced with a bill referring to what is still one of the most vitally important subjects for all Canadians, namely, housing.
It was on January 28 that the house gave second reading to this bill. In the meantime the bill has been submitted to what I believe I may fairly call exhaustive study on the part of the standing committee on banking and commerce. That committee proceeded to its task with diligence. In the period between February 2, when it held its first meeting on the bill, and March 2 when it concluded its labours on the bill and reported it with a number of amendments that committee held, if my reckoning is correct, no fewer than 23 meetings. In my experience of 85 years as a member of the banking and commerce committee I do not recall any case where that committee has given more careful and constructive study to any measure laid before it than it did to Bill 102. There has been no evidence whatever of partisan considerations in that committee, but the desire evidenced on all hands was to make this bill as good and as effective a piece of legislation as was possible within the principle of the bill as approved by the house on second reading.
The chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Spadina, is I believe also deserving of commendation for the way in which he presided over the sittings of the committee, and for his conduct of the affairs of the committee. While we did not agree on all matters, nevertheless he did contribute to the atmosphere of co-operation which prevailed.
The committee has heard extensive evidence. That evidence has not been printed

National Housing Act as yet in its entirety, Mr. Chairman, and perhaps it is regrettable that the house, now in committee of the whole, is dealing with this matter without having before it all the evidence taken in that committee. It is probably a fair estimate that the evidence when printed in its entirety will extend to something like 600 printed pages, all in small print at that.
The evidence was drawn from many very competent witnesses representing organizations whose views are entitled to be treated with respect on the part of that committee and this house. No doubt the principal witness was Mr. Mansur, the very able president of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. It is not the first time that Mr. Mansur has appeared before the banking and commerce committee as a witness. The committee heard him at very considerable length two years ago when it reviewed the operations and reports of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I believe this tribute is due to Mr. Mansur. He has always shown himself to be a well informed, willing and co-operative witness. His answers were clear and they always impressed the committee as being frank. I believe the committee is much indebted to Mr. Mansur for the evidence which he tendered to it at many of the 23 meetings which were held.
We also heard evidence, Mr. Chairman, from representatives of such organizations as the Dominion Mortgage and Investments Association, represented by its president, Mr. John T. Bryden. We heard from Mr. Atkinson, president of the Canadian Bankers Association, and from Mr. Graham Towers, the governor of the Bank of Canada. We also heard from representatives of the three national labour organizations, and from representatives of the Canadian Construction Association, the Canadian Home Builders' Association, the Canadian Association of Mayors and Municipalities, the Co-operative Union of Canada and others.
In all cases, Mr. Chairman, the evidence given was of very substantial assistance to the committee and through the committee to the entire House of Commons.
Organizations of this kind and their representatives perform a most useful public service in placing before a parliamentary committee the fruits of their study of a measure of this kind and the important subject upon which it is based.
Let me turn back to put in its setting the position in which the house found itself after giving this measure second reading on January 8. In saying this, Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to reopen the debate on second


reading. What I propose to do is to put in its setting what occurred then and to lead up to what I hope will be a constructive review of some of the evidence submitted to the committee, much of which is confirmatory of the views which some of us sought to place before the house on second reading, and other parts of the evidence of interest on other accounts.
The procedure of this house requires that even in a bill of a technical nature in which the principle is not easily isolated or identified, that principle must nevertheless be approved before the bill is submitted to a detailed study in the committee to which it is referred, whether the reference is to the committee of the whole or to one of the select committees of the house.
I believe the procedure followed in another place does not involve that same approval in principle on second reading before the bill is given detailed study in a committee, and there are occasions when such a procedure, it seems to me, has a definite value. It would have value on a bill of this kind which is largely a technical bill, which covers a vast territory, and which by common agreement was to be referred after second reading to the standing committee on banking and commerce for detailed study and review.
On second reading, Mr. Chairman, the point of view of the official opposition was put forward-and I think I am summarizing it fairly-in a manner which was designed to enable us to discharge our duty as an opposition by scrutinizing that bill very closely and by seeking to compare it as far as was then possible with the accomplishments under the legislation which it was proposed to replace. We sought to expose what we believed to be the dangers involved in the bill, acknowledging at the same time benefits that were held out for the bill by those who introduced it. We sought in a fair and, I hope, constructive way to put the bill in such a setting that its value could be measured not in terms of the propaganda which had been built up around it, but in terms of its true merits. It was recognized that the bill, in the great majority of its provisions, was simply a re-enactment of existing provisions of the National Housing Act and it was on that basis, Mr. Chairman, and I want to lay emphasis on this, that we of the official opposition voted for the bill on second reading in order to approve what we considered to be the principle of the bill.
It was a little surprising that, despite that frank and, I hope, constructive way in which we approached the bill, and made our position known for the four days during which this

bill was debated on the motion lor second reading, hon. members opposite should shout in derision when we voted for the bill on second reading as though there was something inconsistent in the position which we had taken in voting for that bill on second reading. The official opposition was completely consistent with the position which it had taken on that bill.
Whatever may have been our feeling about the way in which hon. members opposite conducted themselves when the vote was being taken on second reading, let me emphasize, sir, that it did not affect our position in the committee. We went into that committee, and I am quite sure the chairman and other hon. members of that committee will readily acknowledge this, with a completely constructive attitude. There were no partisan considerations evident in that committee, so far as I am aware, at any time.
The desire shared by all members of the committee, regardless of party, was to report back to the house as effective a measure as could be devised within the powers given to the committee with respect to Bill No. 102. The bill has now come back to the house, which is now sitting in committee of the whole, with a number of amendments which I think, in all cases, can be described as technical amendments. In these amendments there has been no interference with the essence of the bill or with the nature of the new scheme that is proposed therein.
Let us then consider this bill in relation to the underlying purpose of it. The purpose indicated in the debate on second reading and before the committee can, I think, be fairly classified under two headings. Broadly speaking, the purpose of the bill is to maintain the rate of house construction in Canada which last year reached a round figure of
100,000	housing units and, if possible, to increase that figure. The second aspect of the purpose of the bill is to bring it within the reach of more Canadians to build houses for their own occupancy. Therefore the question which the committee must ask itself at this stage is whether, in the light of the knowledge that we now possess, the bill is likely to accomplish this purpose of a twofold nature.
One of the first questions put to Mr. Mansur-and I am dealing now with the latter aspect of the purpose of the bill, namely to bring it within the economic power of more Canadians to build their own houses-was what would be, in his estimation, the increase in the number of those within the band of effective economic demand as a result of the enactment of this bill with its provision for
National Housing Act
reducing the down payment and lengthening the amortization period of mortgages. I consider his answer must be regarded as setting the boundary within which we must approach the whole question. I think it is correct to say that Mr. Mansur's answer came as a surprise to many of us, in view of the elaborate build-up the bill has had. His answer was that the bill would enlarge existing effective economic demand in Canada for homes by between 5,000 and 15,000 persons.
That answer is to be measured as against further testimony of Mr. Mansur. He was asked what is today the effective economic demand for houses; in other words, what is the number of Canadians who want to build houses under the provisions of the National Housing Act and who have the means today to meet the existing terms as to down payment, income and so forth. His answer was 120,000.
In order to see this bill in its true perspective, Mr. Chairman, we must realize that what Mr. Mansur was saying was that if the bill is enacted you will increase the number of those who are today in the field, qualified under the act and able to purchase within its terms, by between 5,000 and 15,000. Let us take the middle figure for percentage purposes and let us say it is 10,000. That would represent an increase of 10,000 on top of an existing number of 120,000. Therefore it means an increase of something between 8 per cent and 8J per cent.
Accordingly, Mr. Chairman, when we look at the bill in the light of that important evidence, I think it becomes immediately apparent that the bill is not going to work all the wonders that some-and particularly some hon. members opposite in their speeches on second reading-held out for it. The pictures that were drawn of the new heaven and the new earth that was suddenly going to be created following the introduction of this bill and the new scheme of insured loans just does not stand against the evidence given by Mr. Mansur, who was a most capable and informed witness. I say that not in any hostile sense, Mr. Chairman; far from it. I say it with a view to asking this committee of the whole house to consider the bill in its true proportions, stripped of a lot of the propaganda that has been built up around it from government sources.
Let us now examine the means by which the existing band of economic demand is to be enlarged. The two methods put forward are, first of all, a reduction in the down payment and, second, the extension of the period for repayment of principal. I am not going to dwell on those aspects because

National Housing Act
I am sure the terms of the measure are well known to the committee. So far as the down payment is concerned, I think what has been said on the other side of the chamber in relation to the measure must be compared with what I have just recalled of the evidence of Mr. Mansur. As to the extension of the period of amortization from the present period of twenty years to a maximum period of thirty years, it is quite evident that the extension of the time will help to increase the number of economic purchasers, as will indeed the provision for reducing the down payment. But let us remember that extending the period of amortization increases, in the aggregate, the carrying charges. Let us also bear this point in mind because I think it is something that is of crucial importance, and I propose to say a little bit more about it when I come to the subject of interest. Simply because there is an extension of the period of amortization from the present twenty years to a maximum of thirty years, we cannot assume that there will necessarily be any reduction in the amount of the monthly payment. Let us also bear this further point in mind. With the reduction in the down payment, there will be a corresponding increase in the mortgage. Let us bear in mind also that if there is an increase in the rate of interest you are going to have a situation where, depending upon the amount, the monthly payments could actually increase under the present bill.
Having made those passing comments on the problem of bringing it within the power of more Canadians to qualify for home purchase under the act, let me turn now to what has become, in the light of the bill, a matter of the highest importance. When the Prime Minister made his announcement of this measure on October 1, he indicated that the purpose of the legislation, when introduced, would be to increase the supply of funds available for loan on mortgage security. He took account of the present prevailing high rate of home construction in Canada-running in 1953, as I have said, to a figure of about 100,000 units per year- and said that it would be necessary to find new sources of mortgage funds if the necessary financing to sustain a home construction program of that size were to be assured. The scheme of insured mortgages is the government's answer along with the enlargement of the group of approved lending institutions by the inclusion therein for the first time in Canada's history of the chartered banks and Quebec savings banks. No one in Canada, in fact, no one on this globe, can say with certainty what will be the result

of the enactment of this bill so far as sources of mortgage funds are concerned. We can simply take the evidence that has been put before us and weigh it, recognizing that it is based largely upon estimate and opinion.
The first result of the bill will be the abolition of the joint loans under the present part I of the National Housing Act. That will immediately result in the withdrawal from the supply of available mortgage funds of $60 million per annum which the government now is contributing through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to the total now available. Therefore we must be assured that under this measure there will be at least $60 million of new funds available, and we hope more, for there would be little use in tearing up the present National Housing Act and replacing it with another if there were not reasonable assurance of a substantial increase over that $60 million per annum from funds available from new sources.
The great bulk of mortgage funds available hitherto has come from the approved lending institutions consisting of the life, loan and trust companies in Canada. The evidence tendered on their behalf before the committee indicates that we may expect, subject to payment of attractive interest rates, a continuation also of approximately the same volume of mortgage funds as they have made available in record amounts in recent years. They do not foresee an increase in funds available. They consider that they are now lending to the limit on mortgage security. The question was asked: Will there be other new sources? Is there any indication that funds will perhaps be available from outside Canada which have not hitherto been available from foreign sources? Mr. Mansur was able to tell us that there had been some inquiries from foreign capital, which might indicate that there is some little possibility at any rate that funds may be attracted into this country for investment in mortgages under the provisions of this bill which may not have hitherto been available. As things stand now, those are only inquiries.
But it is quite clear, Mr. Chairman, that the house must depend principally upon the chartered banks for new sources of mortgage funds to replace first of all the $60 million of government money which will not now be contributed to the pool of mortgage funds, and to augment the total after that. I wish to be fair in my treatment of the evidence on this very important aspect of the bill. Let us recognize in the first place that insured loans, that is, mortgage loans

insured by a government agency, are something absolutely new in Canadian experience. The United States has had a form of insured mortgage loans under federal legislation, but for Canada this is something quite new, and only time will tell the extent to which the insurance feature of this scheme will have the effect of attracting sources of capital. Time will be needed to measure public reaction, the reaction of sources of capital, and the usefulness of the scheme in general.
Let us recognize, sir, that there are disagreeable tasks accompanying the enforcement of the mortgage security. Under the bill there is no claim open to any mortgagee holding an insured loan unless he delivers title and possession to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. That undoubtedly will require in all cases either foreclosure or acquisition of the title of the mortgagor by quit claim deed. Those tasks are not very attractive to any mortgagee, particularly if this is new in his experience. The prospect of moratorium legislation or debt adjustment legislation in the event of a recession in Canada looms very high, and the effect of moratorium legislation or debt adjustment legislation would be to put it beyond the power of any mortgagee holding an insured loan to deliver title and possession and thereby qualify himself to make a claim for payment under the insurance guarantee on the part of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
I come directly now to the question of what we may expect from the chartered banks of Canada by way of funds for this new type of mortgage. This, I take it, is in the last analysis the crux of the bill. We are looking to the possibility of sustaining the rate of house construction in Canada of
100,000	units a year. We hope to increase that. The capacity of the Canadian house building industry was described to us as somewhere in the neighbourhood of 125,000 units. Very well. Let us then examine the evidence on this point. Mr. Atkinson, the president of the Canadian Bankers Association, was their spokesman. He brought a brief which he said had been submitted to all members of the association, which includes all the chartered banks of Canada, and he said he had no doubt that they subscribed to the brief and the views which he put before the committee.
These are the facts which are outstanding in the evidence of Mr. Atkinson in relation to the vital question of what the banks are likely to contribute to the pool of mortgage funds. First, the banks were not consulted
National Housing Act
before this legislation was announced. Second, the banks did not seek legislation of this kind nor the power to lend money on the security of real estate. Third, there is no enthusiasm on the part of the banks made evident in any degree for the scheme of the bill. Fourth, Mr. Atkinson did express genuine concern about the effect on the public relations of the banks if they are obliged, as an incident of realizing on these insured loans, to foreclose on the homes of people who undoubtedly in a large number of cases will be their own customers. He did not relish the effect on the banks' public relations of having to take that course.
Fifth, this is an entirely new field in the experience of Canadian bankers, and Mr. Atkinson was extremely cautious in many of the opinions he expressed because, as he said, he was not qualified to do so, having had no experience whatsoever in the field of mortgages on real estate. Mr. Graham Towers in his evidence recognized that this is, in the words of the expression used on page 269 of the proceedings and evidence of the committee, "a radical departure" from Canadian banking legislation and Canadian banking practice hitherto.
Sixth, let me say a word about the use that will be made of bank branches. The picture has been drawn for us that with
4,000	bank branches in Canada there will be 4,000 local mortgage lending offices.
Well, sir, that may be a very pretty picture, but it does not accord with the evidence given on behalf of the banks by Mr. Atkinson. While assuring us that the banks would do their best to make this scheme work, he did say that, while the local branches of the banks will receive these applications for loans, there is going to be very extensive supervision exercised by the banks from their regional offices, usually one in each province. If one looks at the evidence on page 301, it will be seen that Mr. Atkinson is saying that most of these mortgages, once up into the figures into which most of them are going to run, around $8,000, are going to be referred to the regional bank office for approval before the local bank manager will be able to give an answer to the applicant for the mortgage loan.
On the subject of co-operation, Mr. Chairman, Mr. Atkinson confirmed what everyone knew he could expect, namely that the banks would co-operate. The Canadian banks are such that, and I think this should be said to their credit, their co-operation in matters of public policy on any proper subject is assured. I said when I spoke on second reading that we could be assured of that co-operation. My

National Housing Act words to that effect are recorded on page 1329 of Hansard for January 21, 1954. I said, "I know we can assume that the banks will co-operate". Speaking later, the hon. member for Brantford, as recorded at page 1344 of Hansard for the same day, said:
The hon. member for Eglinton thought that the banks would not co-operate . . .
His statement, of course, had no basis whatever in fact. It was completely without foundation, and indeed was the very opposite of what I had said. Let there be no doubt about it. It was said on behalf of the banks of Canada that they would endeavour to make this scheme work. There can be no doubt about that.

maintopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT
subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: It is to their profit, undoubtedly.

maintopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT
subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
The hon. member says it would be to their profit.	It must be
remembered that we are dealing with a measure here which depends for its success very largely upon making this new form of investment attractive to those who have capital. Unless we recognize that fact, we can finish up legislating to provide for a scheme of mortgages which would fail to attract that capital that is going to be necessary to make the scheme work. When one talks, as I shall have occasion to do in a moment, about some of the features of this scheme, let us be quite frank with one another and let us recognize that one does not say these things with a view to mollycoddling any particular holder of capital. One says these things with a view to recognizing the realities of the situation, and to show that unless these mortgages are sufficiently attractive to capital then the whole scheme under the act could prove abortive. We could finish up with a situation where we were worse off than we are under the present act.
Before I leave that subject let me stress this. The present act has produced substantial accomplishments. There is no hon. member in this house who can contend with any degree of success that the present act has broken down or has proven a failure. On the contrary, the evidence that was adduced before the committee went to show that the accomplishments of the present act have been substantial; it has worked well. The scheme of joint loans under part I of the present act has been successful. I, for one, Mr. Chairman, do not wish to see us reaching out for shadows and giving up the substance of the present act unless I can be very sure the new bill does offer substantial advantages over what I know to be the existing advantages of the present act.


The eighth point in the evidence tendered on behalf of the banks was that the funds of the banks are now fully employed. Indeed, Mr. Atkinson said, "We are now relatively fully loaned". I am not overlooking the fact that there will be, we trust, new sources or at least there will be new bank deposits in the future. But let us remember that the banks are going to have pressing claims upon them to continue to finance business and industry in the whole broad picture of national development. Whatever funds may be put into the hands of the banks by way of new savings of the Canadian people are not going to be available in their entirety for loans on mortgage securities; let no one believe that.
Let me make this final comment upon the evidence given on behalf of the banks. How much money are the banks likely to put into this pool of mortgage funds in Canada? That is the principal question. The answer, and the only answer I think that can be accurately given to that question in the light of the evidence tendered before the committee, is that the banks are going to be very cautious in their approach. Their participation, certainly in the early stages of this scheme, is going to be limited. Mr. Towers, in his evidence, made it quite clear that, even before it became apparent to him that new sources of mortgage money would be required to sustain the existing program or to enlarge it, he felt that the time had come to remove the strict prohibition upon bank loans on mortgages and real estate. He said that in his opinion the banks would subscribe a fairly modest percentage of the funds available in their hands. At another point he said it would not amount to 25 per cent of the funds in the hands of the banks available for lending. When I pressed him, he said he had just picked that figure out of the air, and was not prepared to say what that figure would be. It was purely a negative statement he had made with regard to that percentage.
I come now to one aspect of this matter on which I think it can be fairly said the Minister of Public Works dwelt with some emphasis in his statements, both during the resolution stage and in his two speeches on second reading of the bill. It was the answer he sought to give to the problem of liquidity. Of course, we realize that the twin problems of security and liquidity facing the banks are different in their nature. The answer to the problem of security, in the view of the government, is the insurance. But let us look at this problem of liquidity. It is a different thing altogether to say that the bank's loan on real estate is secure, because at the same time you must recognize that the bank is

stepping out of a field in which credit is extended for periods up to a maximum of nine months and into a field where the period of the loan extends to a maximum of 30 years. In the face of that situation, even recognizing that the banks' loans on mortgages are quite secure if you will wait for redemption over 30 years, how can we maintain the necessary liquidity that is the essence of the Canadian banking system?
The answer put forward by the government was the provision to be made for financing on the part of the Bank of Canada. And so the committee awaited with no little interest the evidence of Mr. Graham Towers in this respect. I think the evidence of Mr. Towers in this respect was a severe surprise to many members of the committee. Mr. Towers made it abundantly clear at the outset that the Bank of Canada will not buy and will not discount a single insured mortgage. In the second place, the Bank of Canada, on certain terms, will be authorized and will be prepared, on terms acceptable to it, to accept these insured mortgages as collateral. But he said these insured mortgages would not be the first security resorted to by the chartered banks in seeking accommodation on the part of the Bank of Canada.
In the third place, the Bank of Canada reserves the right to refuse to extend that accommodation if it is not satisfied. And while under present conditions one cannot imagine the Bank of Canada refusing, nevertheless who is to say that the circumstances might not drastically change?
And in the fourth place, Mr. Chairman,- and this no doubt was the greatest surprise of all-Mr. Graham Towers said emphatically that the period for which accommodation would be extended to the banks would not be anything like the period of the loans, 30 years, would not be for a year, would not be, if you please, more than a matter of several months, and finally he got down to saying a matter of weeks.
Well, in the light of that evidence, when Mr. Atkinson came to the committee as a witness the following day, naturally we asked him about the use the banks would make of that provision for accommodation, and what value they attached to it. If you will look at page 270 of the evidence, Mr. Chairman, you will see that Mr. Towers sums up the value of this provision for accommodation on the part of the Bank of Canada in these words. My question is at the bottom of page 270, and reads as follows:
Q. Have you formed any estimate or are you prepared to express any opinion as to the extent to which you think the banks may be expected, over a period of one year, or over a few years, to use
National Housing Act
their portfolios of insured mortgage loans as collateral with the Bank of Canada?-A. Oh, I would say very little.
Then, further on, at page 302 where Mr. Atkinson replied to a previous question as to this same matter and said that this provision for accommodation by the Bank of Canada would have very little bearing on the banks' attitude toward taking insured loans, this extract from the evidence follows:
Q. You say it would have no bearing. What value would it have for the banks to be able to get this limited accommodation at the Bank of Canada on these insured mortgages as collateral?-A. From a practical point of view, none.
Q. No value?-A. None.

speechtext: Has the hon. member unanimous consent to continue?

maintopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT

speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT
subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman, and I thank the committee for its courtesy. I am sure, Mr. Chairman, that what I am saying now by way of review will perhaps help to shorten the debate later on; in fact, I can say to the committee that that will be the result.
Now, sir, I leave that subject of liquidity with the observation that in the view of those who are principally concerned, namely, the banks, they attach no value whatever to the right to obtain accommodation from the Bank of Canada on their portfolio of insured mortgage loans for short periods.
I turn now, sir, to a wider question. Naturally this next problem is one that must give us concern. It certainly gave the government concern following the outbreak of hostilities in Korea. I refer to the possibility of inflation. It is the question of pressures resulting from an enlarged demand for what might prove to be a limited supply of houses and materials.
The government has said that the reason it stepped in in 1950 and 1951 to curtail house construction in Canada was that they felt it necessary to do so because of the threat of inflation. Well, sir, this must be a question to engage our consideration. Today the price of houses is high. It is at an all-time height in Canada. It has levelled off in the past year. It might be said that the price of houses and the cost of construction have been stabilized. Nevertheless, Mr. Chairman, I do not think anyone will say that, even in the

National Housing Act
face of that levelling out, we can just accept without concern the high cost of housing in Canada today.
Mr. Mansur has indicated that the existing demand, namely, 120,000 units-and that he said is the effective economic demand-is more than a whole year's output of housing in Canada according to present rates.

maintopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT
subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT
subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT
subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: At page 92 of the evidence Mr. Mansur very clearly points out that the effective demand is now 125,000 to 130,000. Why does the hon. member persist in using a figure that is 10,000 lower than that which Mr. Mansur gave?

maintopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT
subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Well, it is not a figure of
10.000	lower. The figure of 120,000 was used elsewhere. It will be remembered that Mr. Mansur was asked this question in several places. Let me draw my hon. friend's attention to the statement he has just read. Mr. Mansur was asked about the rate at which the market would absorb housing coming on the market at the present time. The answer was:
At the present time new houses, both tor home ownership and rental, are coming in at the rate of about 105,000 units a year. I believe that the effective demand is sufficient to look after new production at the rate of 125,000 to 130,000 units a year.
My hon. friend, was a member of the committee and will recall that when we came to the question of capacity of the house construction industry in Canada, it was put at
125.000	and questions were asked of Mr. Mansur, even up to the last day of testimony, about the ability of the present demand to absorb 125,000 to 130,000 units a year, namely, the full capacity, without appreciable inflation. I think my hon. friend will find that the same figure was not used in all cases. I am not going to take the time now to refer to the figures. As a matter of fact, I am quite prepared, for the purpose of the point I am now making, to take the figure of 125,000 as the existing effective economic demand, but not the housing need. Here we are thinking simply in terms of those who have the means to buy, to qualify under the existing act. I am dealing with the point whether, in the face of the existing demand, if you bring on to the mortgage market another
5.000	to 15,000 persons, heads of families who can qualify under the new provisions, you may expect an upward pressure on existing prices as the result of that enlargement of demand.

I wish here to say, Mr. Chairman, that opinions on this point on the part of the witnesses were not unanimous. Representatives of the Canadian Home Builders' Association and the Canadian Construction Association said that the Canadian market could absorb another 25,000 housing units a year, namely, a total of 125,000, without appreciable inflation. On the other hand, there were witnesses such as Mr. Bryden, president of the Dominion Mortgage and Investments Association, who felt the inevitable effect of enlarging the present effective economic demand would be to exert upward pressures upon the cost of construction in Canada.
There remains the problem of the lack of serviced land. The Minister of Public Works has recognized this quite frankly in several speeches he has made in the house. The lack of serviced land is still the principal bottleneck limiting house construction in Canada. Mr. Mansur referred to this on page 87 of the evidence. This shortage exists in its most acute form in the places where the need is greatest, namely, in areas contiguous to the large metropolitan centres where the housing need is felt most keenly today. This bill contains no new provision in relation to this subject; it simply re-enacts the present provisions.
I leave this subject with the observation which I have made not a few times in this house, that we are not going to grapple effectively with the problem of the lack of serviced land until something really concrete is done to assist the municipalities in this country who are compelled, in the face of rising costs, to limp along with the same sources of revenue which they were given in 1867.
The problem of rural housing was of concern to the committee and I assure you that that concern was not confined to hon. members representing rural ridings. The fact of the matter is that only insignificant use has been made of the provisions of the housing act to assist rural housing. At page 59 of the proceedings Mr. Mansur is reported as having said:
The result Is that the loans on the farms have been much more in the field of maintenance and improvement than in the new construction field. We have made, I think, only about eight farm loans in the last six or seven years.
And again:
There just does not seem to be any demand for loans for new farm houses. The actual number, sir, is nineteen farm loans.
So far as farm loans are concerned, the bill has no special provisions. The provisions in relation to loans on farm homes are the same as those for city homes. The problem

remains one of willingness on the part of the lending institutions to lend money for the construction of farm homes and, on the other hand, the existence of an effective economic demand.
With regard to slum clearance, a very important question, there is no new treatment under this bill except in one particular. The bill re-enacts the provisions of the existing act in precisely the same form with one change. Instead of referring to the kind of conditions that the legislation proposes to grapple with after a fashion as slums, substandard and dilapidated housing conditions, the word "slum" is now omitted and we find that the statutory description is confined to dilapidated or substandard housing conditions. Whatever may be the sufficiency of the reason for eliminating the word, let us realize that simply by taking the word "slum" out of the National Housing Act we are not doing one thing to grapple with the problem of slum clearance.
This problem of slum clearance must receive more attention in all parts of Canada than it has hitherto. Something very frank and wholesome was said on this subject on behalf of the Federation of Mayors and Municipalities in the evidence that was submitted to the committee, in which we find this statement:
There is considerable public apathy with respect to the matter and active opposition to the idea of public housing in some quarters.
It is perhaps because of these considerations that' the federal government itself appears to be somewhat reticent in encouraging the use of those provisions in the National Housing Act whereby a large-scale program of slum clearance and low rental housing could be undertaken.
There is a lot of public apathy in regard to this question. Indeed the matter has been submitted to local electors in some areas and in some cases they have rejected proposals for slum clearance. There are many in this house and elsewhere who make a habit of throwing brickbats at the city of Toronto. As an unrepentant citizen of the city of Toronto I wish to say that I am proud that my city has taken the lead in this respect and that the Regent Park project has set a standard, an example which, if followed in other parts of Canada where similar conditions exist, would create beneficial results.
I had the privilege of being a member of the civic body in Toronto, the city planning board, which in 1943 made the first concrete recommendation for the establishment in the area bounded by Parliament, Dundas, River and Gerrard streets in Toronto of a housing project to replace existing slums. I think that enterprise has been a credit to the city of Toronto and it sets an example which I commend to other municipalities.
National Housing Act

speechtext: I assure you that we cannot say the same thing for Montreal.

maintopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT

speechtext: My hon. friend will have to speak for his own city. I am simply commenting on what I think has been a salutary example. May I say also that this question was first submitted to the electors of the city of Toronto who approved of the proposal by a substantial majority.

maintopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT
subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: A good thing.

maintopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT
subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Let me say in passing that a very effective presentation was made to the committee on behalf of the Co-operative Union of Canada. The bill contains no change in the provisions of the existing act with respect to co-operative housing. The minister did say why in his opinion the request of the Co-operative Union should not be granted. Their request was that they should be accorded the same terms as are now available to limited dividend housing corporations in the matter of interest rates and the period of amortization. I think members of the committee felt that something should be done to encourage co-operative housing. Certainly the statement made to the committee in support of co-operative housing was an impressive one.
Finally in this review of matters that were considered I should like to report to the committee of the whole, as the evidence of the committee on this point has not yet been printed, that when the minister was asked when the government proposes to proclaim the provisions of part IV of the act in relation to home improvement and home extension loans he indicated that the government is not prepared to do so at the present time but would review the situation in six months' time to see to what extent funds made available for the assistance of housing were fully employed. I think we shall all hope that it will be possible for the government to proclaim the provisions of part IV of the housing act soon. Parliament does not like legislating, I am sure, provisions that are simply permitted to remain a nullity.
I am trying to hurry to a conclusion, Mr. Chairman. This bill, if recognized for what it is, is to a substantial degree simply enabling legislation. It proposes to confer the widest powers on the governor in council to pass regulations, regulations which will be essentially legislative in nature. This should concern us. We are not legislating fully in passing this measure; to a considerable degree we are legislating in the dark. We are legislating in terms of what in many important respects is simply a skeleton measure. We sought information as to what

maintopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT
subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, perhaps at this point I should rise on a question of privilege. I know my hon. friend will wish to be corrected. I made that matter perfectly clear in my speech on second reading of the bill. I made it clear that I was not taking credit for the government nor taking credit for the legislation. I said housing was an effort on the part of all Canadians concerned therewith. I must say at the same time that the minute there is a downturn, then the responsibility is placed on the shoulders of the government and blame is attributed to the legislation.

maintopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT
subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am happy to have the statement made by the minister this afternoon. It makes the matter perfectly clear as far as I am concerned, and I shall say no more on that score. I simply make this clear because the impression I formed, as I said, when the minister was speaking, was that of

National Housing Act
too much "we". As he realizes, I am referring to what he said on page 1572 of Hansard. In view of what the minister has now said, I will say no more about it.
This is my final word, Mr. Chairman. We wish to see houses built. We will give every opportunity to any measure that holds out any hope of providing more houses for Canadians, by proper schemes and sensible undertakings. In keeping with the careful scrutiny that we have given to this measure, we will continue to apply careful and, I hope, co-operative and constructive scrutiny to the administration which the bill will receive at the hands of the government.

maintopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT
subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I just make one interjection before the next hon. member who speaks takes the floor? I wish to refer to the page of Hansard of which the hon. member for Eglinton was good enough to remind me, namely page 1572. In reply to a question by the hon. member for Eglinton in which he said:
I think the minister will agree that not all were under the act.
I said as follows:
X readily agree with that, Mr. Speaker, and I have said so. This is an effort by all Canadians who are concerned with the house building business, encouraged, aided and abetted by the government under the terms of the National Housing Act.

maintopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT
subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: That was a big rider you added.

subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.

subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Would the hon. member
answer a question? Is the figure of 50 per cent not based on the fact that they will apply for a maximum loan on a $10,000 house?

National Housing Act

maintopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT
subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: It is reasonable to assume that they would have to apply for maximum loans because their income is so small they could do nothing else. They have little savings.

maintopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT
subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: But do you not think you should qualify that statement because they can get smaller loans if they make their down payment larger?

maintopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT
subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
My hon. friend says that they can get smaller loans. Surely that is very academic in view of the cost of living today and the fact that the normal family must find it extremely difficult to exist on $3,000, let alone save money to increase their down payment. The minister said in the house that whereas stimulation and assistance for housing can come from the federal government, in the final analysis it is the municipality which decides the amount of housing to be built. There is a regrettable element of buck-passing in this matter because today municipalities in Canada are finding themselves increasingly squeezed owing to the financial conditions under which they operate. Into municipalities around the area where I live are coming new families with children who are occupying new homes. The municipalities have got to provide services, sewer, water and police services, perhaps even hospital services, roads, and of course educational facilities. I find that municipalities are faced with the problem of having to decide to build either roads or schools. They cannot afford both even if they can afford one, and such is not always the case.
Are these municipalities going to look with assurance on still further additions to housing in their areas when they find that their financial means are such that they cannot service those already there? I do not think so, not unless the government changes its policy and decides to come to the rescue of municipalities by making long term low interest loans for the purpose of providing the ordinary amenities of life such as education and other necessities. If that is not done the response of the municipalities will of necessity be a negative one.
I assume that one of the purposes of this legislation is to make the rate for lending more attractive. Fears have been continually expressed that the supply of funds is drying up. We were told that the insurance companies already have 30 per cent of their assets in mortgages. At page 1314 of Hansard of January 21 the minister said:
... it has become increasingly clear that at some stage they would have to reduce their rate of new mortgage lending from its recent level.

Later he said that a decline in mortgage money from this source must be anticipated. There is going to be a decline, and what is the government's answer, in part, under this legislation? It is to make that decline even worse by taking away the quarter share of the guaranteed loan. That is not an answer for which I have any appreciation. In the committee Mr. Mansur said that financing in 1953 would depend on the continued willingness of the life companies to increase then-relative holdings of mortgages. The increase last year made possible the expenditure of about $95 million. The life companies were willing, Barkis was willing last year, but what of this year and what of the years to come? If the companies decided not to increase their ratio, if indeed the companies decided to decrease their ratio of mortgages, then from what source would we get the additional funds?
Mr. Mansur said there is no substantial source of private mortgage funds available under present arrangements to provide an offset. Yet, what is the government's solution? It is to cut out their quarter, to cut out their payment of $60 million spent on acquiring homes. Mr. Mansur said again under the new arrangement the quarter share provided under joint loans by Central Mortgage will no longer be available. That is not an answer, as I said, that I understand or appreciate. Mr. Bryden said in the committee that the number of units financed will decrease by the abandonment of joint lending. Under this part of its policy the government is going to decrease the number of units; the government's answer is to reduce the money available from government sources for home building.
Obviously then it has to find some other source of money. As the minister said, it is quite clear if there is to be an increase in home building additional funds must come from somewhere other than the present source of institutional mortgage funds. Then, someone in the government had an idea, a revolutionary idea. He looked at the banks' reserves; he looked at the banks' liquid position and said: Boy, here we have got it. The banks are going to supply the money. We will pass legislation and get out of the business; leave it to free enterprise and everybody will be happy. We will put the banks in the real estate field, and we will revolutionize everything in Canada; we will get started on free enterprise home building.
The announcement about the banks being allowed to advance money on real estate was made in October by the Prime Minister. One can only assume that in Montreal the topless towers of Ilium quivered and shook. I suggested to Mr. Atkinson that the banks were

rocked to their foundations by this drastic change in policy. His answer was that he would not agree that they were rocked to their foundations, but he was surprised. For a usually conservative banker to admit surprise is, I would say, equivalent to a lesser person saying he was thoroughly shaken. However, the government sugared the pill.
On page 1316 of Hansard for January 21, 1954, the minister said:
In the matter of liquidity, as I mentioned earlier, it is proposed to make insured mortgages eligible security for Bank of Canada advances to banks in the same way as government bonds.
What did these ungrateful bankers do? They spat the pill out. They did not like it. Mr. Atkinson said he was confident it was not the intention that the central bank should carry for an indefinite period these mortgages as security for loans to banks. When he was asked, as the member for Eglinton pointed out, about their value as collateral, Mr. Atkinson said that, from a practical point of view, there was none. So much for the government's policy.
Then, what were the reasons for asking the banks to go into this field? I think the minister told us when he spoke of the widespread branch system, and of the 4,000 branches stretching from coast to coast. Perhaps the government envisages queues of potential borrowers lining up before the banks to get money to build homes. The evidence given by Mr. Atkinson must have poured cold water on the government's idea, if nothing else, for Mr. Atkinson informed us that very few of his branch managers were entitled to lend even as much as $10,000 without reference to a regional supervisor.
Then Mr. Atkinson said also, dealing with the type of loan, that he thought the banks would not attempt to make loans which they felt were likely to go into default. I am convinced that is true. The only money the banks are going to lend is on such gilt-edged loans that there will be very little risk. I cannot conceive, under this legislation, a worker in my constituency being able to go to the Bank of Montreal and say, "I want $8,000 for a house", and getting it. I do not think it is practical under our present banking system.
What was the banks' answer in case there should be a default? Let the government take the "rap"; that was all there was to it. Mr. Atkinson agreed the government should stay out of business. Mr. Atkinson agreed the banks should be allowed to make profits without government interference. But when it came to losses, Mr. Atkinson agreed that the representatives of the people of Canada should stand the losses for the banks, and
National Housing Act
leave the banks to take the gravy. It is not a system to which the C.C.F. adheres, but of course it is the regular free enterprise system which we happen to oppose.
Now, one of the reasons for going to the banks was their liquidity. I suggested again to Mr. Atkinson that the banks' position was very good; that the banks were drowning in liquidity, but naturally he did not quite see eye to eye with me on that. Mr. Towers said the banks could make up the deficiency for the government's quarter share in the joint loans. Mr. Towers was quite certain of that He thought it could come, in part, from savings deposits. There is about half a billion in savings deposits in Canada today, not all available for loan; let us admit that. Mr. Towers was pressed as to what percentage might be available, and thought 50 per cent was most immodest and 25 per cent perhaps a little less immodest. We could not pin him down to any specific figure. I suggested 10 per cent of savings deposits. Mr. Atkinson in his evidence thought 10 per cent was still high, and that the banks could not possibly reach that amount for some considerable time.
Mr. Towers thought that a moderate percentage of savings deposits would not impair the liquidity of the banks. Again, we asked for a definition of "moderate", but there was none. We asked for a definition of "modest", but there was none. I do not have it in me to blame Mr. Towers, although I should like to have some sort of a definition. Mr. Towers agreed that at least $60 million a year advanced by the banks would not be overly much. Mr. Atkinson subscribed to that idea, and thought $60 million was well within the capabilities of the banks. By a happy coincidence, I suggested that the sum of 6 per cent of the savings deposits was what the banks would perhaps feel inclined to lend over a long period. This 6 per cent would be about $300 million and if that was put up over a period of, say, five years, it would be about $60 million a year. By another odd coincidence, $300 million was the hypothetical figure which Mr. Towers pulled out of the air when he was discussing this matter. My only point in stressing this is to suggest the banks are going, in their own mind, to fix a percentage of the savings deposits that they will be prepared to lend in total. When they reach that percentage, they are not going to go any farther. In other words, the borrowing from the banks is not going to be indefinitely recurring, except in so far as there is a revolving amortization fund and in so far as there are increasing savings deposits.
There again, there is a disagreement amongst the experts, and who am I to enter

I should like to add my voice to this debate at this time. At the outset, I want to say that in my experience in this house of over 19 years this committee was one of the most effective I have ever sat on. I say that because the evidence given by the witnesses on all occasions was straightforward. They gave the very best evidence they could. In most instances they did not hesitate to add their own opinions, and because of that it was a very successful committee. They had a difficult problem to deal with, a problem which most
National Housing Act
of us in this committee and most of the people in the country agree is most disturbing.
Bill No. 102 endeavours to deal with the national housing problem. The government hope that through the medium of this bill they will be able to stimulate house building in the country. I said on another occasion in this house that I did not think the bill would do what the government expect it will do, and I am still of the same opinion. One of the main things upon which the government is basing its hopes is the fact that by bringing the chartered banks into this field a greater amount of money will flow into the construction of houses. I shall speak on that a little later on. The Quebec savings banks are being brought in.
It is possible that with the addition of the chartered banks and the Quebec savings banks some additional money will be found.
I suggest to the government at this time that they go one step further and permit the provincial government treasury branches of Alberta to participate as well, on the same conditions. Whether the inclusion of the banks will accomplish what the government hopes remains to be seen. There are some changes in Bill 102 which will have serious effects. One which I would just note for the moment is that this bill will assist people in the income brackets of over $3,000 a year, but I am positive it is not going to increase home ownership by people in the income brackets of less than $3,000 a year. As I said when talking on this bill on another occasion, it is the people in the low income brackets we should concern ourselves with more than those in the higher income brackets. Those in the higher income brackets could participate under the old set-up. I do not think there will be any improvement in that respect under the new bill.
Then there is the provision for a lower down payment, reducing it from $2,000 to $1,400 on a $10,000 house where the lending value is $8,000. That is going to be of some assistance and will permit a few more people to participate in this plan than was the case heretofore. Then there is the longer amortization period of 25 to 30 years. That will reduce the monthly payments but it will increase the indebtedness, and in the long run the ordinary person is going to pay for his house almost double what he would pay if he had the cash to build it himself.
Then there is the possibility-and I use the word "possibility" advisedly-of better inspection. That to my mind is probably the most important point in building a house, outside of financing. It caused probably more

National Housing Act
trouble in the past than any other single factor. Mr. Mansur was quite frank in his evidence before the committee when he said he was not entirely satisfied with the inspections in the past, but hoped the new bill would bring about some improvement. I do not hesitate to say at this point that I think perhaps the new bill will bring about some improvement in this regard.
Then there will be higher interest rates for the loan companies. That is good for the loan companies, but it is not so good for the people in the lower income brackets. There is a better guarantee for the loan companies, which is charged up to the borrower and for which he gets nothing in return except the privilege of getting a loan.
This brings us to the over-all question of whether this bill will result in stimulating house building. As I said a moment ago, it is hoped that the banks will come to the government's assistance. I should like to refer at this point to the evidence appearing on page 291 of the proceedings of the committee. Some of the sections to which I intend to refer may have been referred to by others, but I think to refer to them again would only serve to bring out the point I wish to bring out. At page 291 of the evidence Mr. Atkinson, vice-president and general manager of the Royal Bank of Canada, who appeared for the mortgage companies and banks concerned, had this to say:
When it was announced by the Prime Minister on October 1 last and simultaneously advised to the banks on the same day by the Minister of Finance, we had not any prior knowledge that such a move was being considered by the government. As I have intimated, such a move would not, I think, have been sought by the banks, particularly at the present time, when the chartered banks in Canada are relatively fully loaned-certainly in our own case it would not have been sought.
The point I want to make there is that according to Mr. Atkinson the banks are relatively fully loaned. Under the present set-up, therefore, the banks will not be in position to make money available under this plan. I should like to refer to what the minister said on December 16 in dealing with this very point, and I quote from page 998 of Hansard:
Later in this session my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), will place the Bank Act and the Bank of Canada Act before the house for revision, when it is proposed to make insured mortgages eligible security for Bank of Canada advances to chartered banks, as is the present position in respect to government bonds.
I do not think I am wrong in assuming that what the Minister of Public Works had in mind then was that more money was going to be made available to the banks, in addition to what they already had, in order

to assist in this house building program. If I am not right I hope he will correct me at this moment. That was the interpretation I placed upon it when I was speaking to this measure some time ago. Of course that is not going to be the case. If the minister expects that to be the result he is doomed to disappointment. Mr. Graham Towers was questioned on this very point by the hon. member for Acadia, and I quote from page 246 of the evidence as follows:
Q. Could you explain just what the provision will be by which additional cash reserves will be made available by the Bank of Canada to chartered banks? Will it be in the form of the purchase of mortgage-or bans against?-A. It won't be in either form, Mr. Quelch. The Bank of Canada, in open market operations in government securities, influences the amount of cash which the banks have. So if we add somewhat to our holdings of securities, as we have in recent times, that puts up bank cash.
The point is that the banks cannot use these insured mortgages to get long-term credits or to increase their cash reserves from the Bank of Canada, and further it will not result in what the minister hopes, because, as Mr. Graham Towers pointed out, if the banks needed money they could use government securities, such as government bonds, and get all the money they needed. But he says, and I have put it on the record already, that the banks are fully loaned, so I am afraid the hopes of the minister are doomed to disappointment. In order to make doubly sure that I am right in this respect I should like to refer to page 270 of the evidence. This has been referred to already, but I refer to it again. Here the hon. member for Eglinton asked this question:
Q. My next question is this: Have you formed any estimate or are you prepared to express any opinion as to the extent to which you think the banks may be expected, over a period of one year, or over a few years, to use their portfolios of insured mortgage loans as collateral with the Bank of Canada?-A. Oh, I would say very little.
Q. Within that small area, is it possible?-A. In fact, perhaps I ought to go further than that and say that I would not expect them to use them at all as security unless they thought it was desirable to do so for psychological reasons.
It is not because they need money but for psychological reasons. I agree with that statement.
Otherwise if they had occasion to borrow funds they would probably put up government bonds because they have plenty of them, and it is a very convenient method of doing it.
Therefore when we are told that under this bill the insured mortgages will be of assistance in financing the construction of homes that is not the case, and the evidence is very clear in that respect.

They will buy bonds and they can do that; and if the chartered banks required the money they have sufficient bonds now which they could sell to the Bank of Canada in order to raise their cash reserves to the degree desired. They do not require insured mortgages for that purpose. The only result of the insured mortgage is to give the lender a greater degree of protection than the 25-75 per cent arrangement which was in force before. Now they have 98 per cent. I believe that statement, that the banks will not and do not intend to use the insured mortgages to increase their cash reserves and thereby make more money available for housing, still stands.
We all know that we really require houses in this country, and the extent of this problem has been referred to on other occasions. As I said before Dr. Forsey on behalf of the C.C.L. gave the estimate that the backlog amounted to 300,000 houses and possibly ran as high as 500,000 houses. Mr. Mansur himself suggested that the backlog in his judgment would run to between 75,000 and 200,000.
If we intend or hope that legislation under Bill No. 102 will maintain the pace which was set last year, at around 105,000 starts, then how can we ever hope to overcome that backlog so the people who really need the houses will get them? It will not be possible under this legislation. I think we will be fortunate if this legislation succeeds in maintaining the present pace, without increasing it. I am certain the government intends that this housing scheme will to a large extent assist in meeting the major unemployment problem which faces us at this moment.
I suggest that anyone who takes advantage of this housing legislation will go into debt
National Housing Act
for 25 or 30 years. Everyone who has already taken advantage of it has gone into debt for a period of 20 or 25 years. That means that unless a policy can be implemented whereby the present unemployment situation will be taken care of, the lending institutions will be faced with the problem of evicting many families. Why? Because they cannot earn sufficient money to pay the monthly charges on the loans they have acquired.
Our biggest concern is not for the people of this country who can afford to build their own houses at the present time, nor are we concerned with those who can afford to pay the high down payments required under this present legislation. Our concern is and should be with those people who cannot afford to come under the housing act, and who have not sufficient income to pay $1,400 as a down payment and then continue to meet high monthly payments over a period of 25 or 30 years.
Dr. Forsey, speaking before the committee, referred to the fact that in June, 1951, about 58 per cent of wage and salary earners were obtaining less than $2,500 per year.
