maintopic: NIAGARA GAS TRANSMISSION LIMITED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is an application by Niagara Gas Transmission Limited, an Ontario company, for authorization to construct, own and operate an extraprovincial pipe line as defined in the Pipe Lines Act, chapter 211 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, and further, that the general Pipe Lines Act will apply to this company. The issued share capital of this company is owned 65 per cent by the Consumers' Gas Company of Toronto and 35 per cent by the Tennessee Gas Transmission Company. Any further issue of capital stock will be in the same ratio, and the balance of funds required will be obtained through the sale of bonds and/or debentures.
The fact is that the Consumers' Gas Company of Toronto is a limited dividend company, incorporated by a special act of the provincial legislature. After ordinary business expenses, allowance for the plant and buildings renewal fund and directors' fees, any surplus remaining goes into a special surplus account which, when it becomes the equivalent of five cents per thousand cubic feet of the amount of gas sold in the previous year, is used to reduce the price of gas.

This special surplus was wiped out in 1933 following a reduction in the price of gas the previous year.
The company has had two other reserves, one established under the act of 1887 of $1 million, and the other arising from the premium received from shareholders on the sale of the capital stock of the company from time to time. The result of recurring deficits over the last 20 years has been that the reserve arising from the premium on capital stock, which was $7,499,680, was reduced by $6,239,871.
For some years the Consumers' Gas Company of Toronto has been fighting a losing battle and in most of the recent years has been forced to dip into its reserve. The cost of manufactured gas has been so great that this company has been gradually pricing itself out of the market. The Toronto city auditor reports that the earnings on the shareholders' investment were 5 * 08 per cent in the year ended September 30, 1952.
The company is authorized by the act of 1887 to pay in dividends 10 per cent on the par value, which was then $100 per share. As from the 1st of January, 1941, the company has been paying 8 per cent, or 80 cents on the present par value of $10 per share. The actual return to individual shareholders depends, of course, on the amount paid for the stock, either from the company treasury or in the stock market. The company has not been permitted since about 1928 to issue rights to existing shareholders. Additional stock must be sold either by auction or tender. The average price received for the stock has ranged from $149 in March, 1932, to $201 per $100 share in February, 1937. Thus the premium on the stock is part of the capital investment. In so far as dividends have tended to reduce the reserve created by this premium, the dividends have been a return of capital.
The directors' fees are limited to $25,000 per year in total. This includes the remuneration to the president, who is not a working president. Two of the directors, the vicepresident and general manager, and the assistant general manager are full-time employees of the company, and presumably receive salaries commensurate with their duties and responsibilities.
The plant and buildings renewal fund, as shown by the report for the year ended September 30, 1953, stood at $9,869,605, compared with investment in plant and equipment and real estate of $31,835,198. This fund arises from the authority of the company to appropriate each year a total of 5 per cent of the value of plant and buildings, but not real estate or unfinished construction. The 83276-1731
Niagara Gas Transmission Limited company has no other provision for depreciation. At the end of 1952 the fund was approximately 32 per cent of the value of plant, buildings and equipment.
When natural gas reaches Toronto the coal gas plant will be obsolete, and it is understood it will be scrapped. The gas holders as well as the water gas sets and the propane plant will be maintained as stand-by units. The equipment to be abandoned, while not new, is, I understand, carried on the books at several million dollars.
The annual report of Consumers' Gas for the year ended September 30, 1953, stated that sales of gas for the 12 months were lower by 4-6 per cent than for the previous year. This was attributed to milder weather. In the first three months of the current fiscal year -that is, October, November, December- sales were again reduced by 4-52 per cent. However, there was an increase in January due to the fact that the average temperature was 8 degrees lower than for January, 1953. The over-all loss of output for four months was 2 per cent.
The sales department of the company, particularly in the house heating division, is very seriously concerned because it is a fact that gas is too expensive under present conditions. The company was holding its business, but not increasing it, in proportion to the increase in population, up to April, 1952, when a further substantial increase in wages resulted in an over-all increase of 25 per cent in the cost of gas. The new rates were calculated on an expected loss of business; and the fact that the company showed a profit for the first full year under the new rates, the first one in 20 years, is due in fact to the inability of householders to quickly change from one kind of cookstove or other appliance to another.
It is estimated that the franchise area of the company now has a population of 1,300,000. The total number of meters divided into that population shows a population of about eight per meter. In contrast, in 1933, when the population of the area was estimated to be 650,000 the population per meter was four persons. The fact is that the manufactured gas business is a dying business. Wages all the way from the coal mine to meter reading have made the price disproportionately high in comparison with electricity, which is untaxed in this province, and with fuel oil which can be delivered at a much lower labour cost.
The 1953 report of the company showed that there are 5,801 shareholders. The average holding is 251 shares. The percentage owned in Canada is 95 per cent, and of the total number of shareholders 55 per cent are
2720	HOUSE OF
Niagara Gas Transmission Limited women. A large part of the stock is owned by insurance companies, which accounts for the fact that there are two insurance company presidents on the board of directors: Mr. J. K. Macdonald of the Confederation Life and Mr. Ross Poyntz of the Imperial Life. The city of Toronto is a shareholder to the extent, I believe, of 15,000 shares.
The company's charter provides that so long as the city owns shares to the par value of $10,000 the mayor shall be ex officio a director of the company and entitled to vote the stock or shares held by the city. A curious feature of the company's charter is the provision whereby no shareholder may have more than ten votes, no matter how many shares he owns. The owner of one share has one vote. I think three shares entitle him to two votes. By the time he gets to the ownership of 20 shares, he has ten votes, and no more.
From the foregoing it is obvious that Consumers' need for a reasonably priced and dependable supply of natural gas to replace the present expensive manufactured gas is urgent and immediate. Unfortunately none of the applicants for an export permit from Alberta to eastern Canada has given Consumers' a definite quotation or has indicated conditions of delivery. It is, of course, impossible to estimate probable gas sales, or sales of any other kind for that matter, unless the price of the product to be sold and delivery conditions are known.
Last year the Consumers' Gas Company made a contract with some United States suppliers in Louisiana and Texas for the purchase of 22,600 million cubic feet of natural gas, this to be transferred to the Niagara river, the international boundary, by Tennessee Gas Transmission Company, and from the centre of the Niagara river by Niagara Gas Transmission Limited, the company making application for this act. At the time this company was formed no authority was required under the Pipe Lines Act, and it was not until the amendment at this session that this application was required.
It is believed by Consumers' Gas Company that the purchase of this gas will be of very great benefit to the consumers in the greater Toronto area. It is believed that natural gas will become directly competitive with oil and will probably be competitive with coal. Because of the very high British thermal unit content of natural gas, and because of the degree to which its heat may be controlled, it is believed that many industries will find it more suitable for their purposes than either coal or oil.
The experience of similar cities in the United States has been that over a period of


a few years the consumption of gas has doubled, and many industries find it economical to use it with small auxiliary appliances to be turned on at times of peak loads during very cold weather. With the present limited production of electric power it is felt that this will be not only economical but of valuable assistance to the people in areas served by this company.
It should be pointed out that the Consumers' Gas Company of Toronto was incorporated by special act of the province of Ontario, which act has been amended a number of times since. As mentioned above, the salaries of the officers and directors are limited. The mayor of Toronto is automatically one of the directors, the dividends to be paid are limited, and when the reserves reach a certain figure the price of gas must be forthwith reduced. The franchise is exclusive to this company for the city of Toronto and for the townships of Toronto, Toronto-Gore, Etobicoke, Vaughan, North York, York, Markham, East York, Scarborough and Pickering, which area of course now includes such municipalities as Forest Hill, Leaside, Swansea, Mimico, New Toronto, Long Branch and Port Credit.
At the time this contract with the United States suppliers and the further contract with Tennessee Gas Transmission Company were made, application was forthwith made to the federal power commission of the United States and authorization was granted for the export from the United States to Canada of this gas. Naturally at that time it was not known that a Canadian pipe line would be built from Alberta to Ontario and Qnebec. Accordingly it was not realized that it might be considered that this contract for United States natural gas might be depriving a Canadian pipe line of one of its major customers. However, a contract has now been made between Tennessee Gas Transmission Company and Consumers' Gas Company of Toronto whereby over the period of the 20-year contract between Consumers' Gas and the United States suppliers, Tennessee Gas Transmission Company will purchase all or any of this gas at any time. This latter contract was made so that if Canadian natural gas is brought to Toronto the Consumers' Gas Company can purchase Canadian gas and dispose of the United States gas for which they have contracted, without any loss to Consumers' Gas.
It is not known at this time how this Canadian gas is to be handled in the province of Ontario and whether a provincial authority will be used for its disposal, but Consumers' Gas Company of Toronto is now in the position that, upon this act being

passed and assuming approval by the board of transport commissioners, they will be able to supply the greater Toronto area with cheap natural gas before the end of this year, and if and when Canadian natural gas becomes available they will be in a position, without loss to themselves on the United States contract, to switch to Canadian natural gas. It is felt, therefore, that the passing of this bill will be of great, immediate and long-term advantage to the Toronto area, and will fit into the Canadian over-all plan to the general benefit of Canada.
It is of course clear to all members of the house that the passing of this act is the embryonic stage in the building of this pipe line. Evidence must still be adduced before the board of transport commissioners showing public convenience and necessity, and to have the location and construction approved. In addition, the company will have to satisfy all provincial legislative requirements and regulations.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: NIAGARA GAS TRANSMISSION LIMITED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what has been explained to us has dealt largely with the immediate requirements of the city of Toronto and the importance of an early supply of natural gas for that large city which is now embraced in the metropolitan organization that has been set up. I submit there is a great deal more to this situation than has been mentioned so far. I am not disagreeing with the facts or figures put forward by the hon. member who is presenting the bill, but I do believe there are very important details which should be in the minds of all members in dealing with the measure now before us.
As has been explained, the bill authorizes the construction of a gas transmission pipe line for the purpose of carrying to the outskirts of the city of Toronto a supply of natural gas from Tennessee, which would then be distributed in the metropolitan area of Toronto by the Consumers' Gas Company. This gas would originate in Tennessee and would flow into a new pipe line to be constructed under the authority of the charter that would be granted by this measure, and then into the servicing lines of the Toronto system.
It has been mentioned already that this in fact is expected to be a temporary arrangement. It was stated the day before yesterday by Mr. A. R. Crozier, the fuel controller of the province of Ontario, that it is expected that within two years there will be a pipe line from western Canada carrying Alberta natural gas to the Toronto field as well as to other parts of eastern Canada.
What is important is the understanding very clearly expressed by Mr. Crozier, the
Niagara Gas Transmission Limited Ontario fuel controller, and the Ontario minister of mines, to whose department Mr. Crozier is attached, that when western gas becomes available the flow will then be reversed through the pipe line to be constructed under the authority of this act, and Canadian gas will be carried to that area in Ontario through which the pipe line will pass coming from Niagara Falls. This, I think, is clearly understood. However, it should be remembered in considering this measure that in expressing their belief that it is desirable that authority be granted for the construction of this pipe line, the Ontario minister of mines and the Ontario fuel controller have both made it clear that this is related to an unqualified condition that this area will be available and will be supplied by gas from western Canada when the Canadian pipe line is constructed.
That being the case, I think we must consider the position in which we find ourselves in dealing with this measure. It is a simple bill of two sections giving general authority to Niagara Gas Transmission Limited to construct, own and operate an extra-provincial pipe line. There are no details as to where the pipe line will be constructed but it is understood by everyone that it will run from the Niagara Falls area to the outskirts of the city of Toronto.
A bill of this kind became necessary as a result of the amendment to the Pipe Lines Act which became law on December 16 last, which required a company to be authorized by a special act of parliament before constructing or operating an extra-provincial pipe line as defined in the amendment. We must remember that whatever is proposed by Ontario or Quebec or any other provincial government is subject to the interprovincial and international authority of the federal government in matters of this kind.
For that reason I feel this government should insist upon an unqualified undertaking that with the construction of an all-Canadian pipe line to eastern Canada, this gas from western Canada, which would then become available, would be used in the area that would be supplied by the pipe line to be constructed under the authority of the proposed measure now before us. I feel it is appropriate that the government give us the assurance that such a condition will be insisted upon during the course of the debate on second reading.
There is more to the measure than simply the construction of a pipe line. There is the broad pattern of the use of natural gas in this country which we cannot deal with in airtight compartments, and which must be regarded as part of the whole mosaic of construction throughout the whole of Canada.
2722	HOUSE OF
Niagara Gas Transmission Limited I have seen statements made, even in the past few days, which suggest there is still in the minds of some people the thought that it is economically unwise to construct an all-Canadian pipe line. I have seen the suggestion that this would create a situation that would be unfair to the producers in Alberta. I hope anything that may be said here will be said with the acceptance of the basic proposition that as Canadians we are having full regard for the future economic welfare of the producers in Alberta and the people of that province, just as we are having regard for the people of eastern Canada who may be served by this project.
In dealing with this subject when that time comes-and this is not the time when the details of this problem can be dealt with-I think we should at all times remember that the price to be paid for natural gas in Alberta should be one that is fair to the producer, that will encourage new exploration and development, and that will afford to those who have risked their capital the reasonable expectation of profit which, in a country that fortunately still supports in the majority a system of free enterprise, will encourage the development there.
No question need arise in connection with this proposal as to the problem of export of gas from Canada or import from the United States. The supplies are enormous, according to the report of the petroleum and natural gas conservation board of Alberta dated November 24 last. It was estimated then that the reserve of natural gas already established in that province as of June 30, 1953, amounted to 11-5 trillion cubic feet. It is established with reasonable certainty that new wells will add at least 3 trillion additional cubic feet each year. These are astronomical figures. Taking those figures and dividing them by the demand that might be reasonably expected, it is expected that they will meet the demands of the local market, the markets of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec who will be very large consumers of that gas, for some time to come.
It may well be that the figures will be higher as time goes on. The figures, however, already established with a high degree of certainty make it clear that the demands of all the provinces to the east, including Ontario and Quebec, can be supplied, and that in addition there can be a substantial export of gas to the United States. For that reason there has been an arrangement under which the company which sought permission to export to the United States has combined its activities with those of the company that applied for permission to build the all-Canadian route. The result of this agreement is


that the present plans contemplate an allCanadian pipe line through the prairie provinces into Ontario and Quebec, as well as a branch pipe line south from Winnipeg to supply the Minneapolis area in the United States. With the added supplies, the amount available for eastern Canada and the United States will doubtless increase.
I mention this now because it is to be hoped that in the consideration of the measure now before us there will be no opposition to the bill on the grounds that it involves importation into Canada from the United States, or any suggestion that in the over-all plans now under consideration there is any objection to that measure of export which can be assured once our own future demands are protected. I would hope that in dealing with this we would have the assurance of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) that it is the intention of the government, with its wide powers over these matters, to insist that the construction of this pipe line carries with it the definite understanding, and in fact the undertaking, that when Canadian gas becomes available and the local market develops as a result of the supply of gas from Tennessee sources, then the market will be supplied by Canadian companies.
I mention that for a definite reason. There are those who believe it is absolutely necessary that a very large consuming area in Toronto and the surrounding districts be part of the area supplied by western Canada if the financing of that development is to be a practical possibility. Concern is also felt by some that this proposal might in some way endanger the construction of the all-Canadian line, unless the most rigid assurances are given. To indicate that this is no idle concern may I mention something I noticed in a quarterly publication called The Heartland, which is published in Washington. I have before me the edition for the fall of 1953. In referring to this development of a pipe line from the Niagara district to Toronto, which would carry Tennessee gas into Toronto, I find on page 50 this statement:
This development is taken to mean the death knell of the all-Canadian project so dear to the federal officials in Ottawa.
I immediately concede that a statement of that kind has no bearing on the prospects; I merely mention it to indicate that there are those who do hold the opinion that this might endanger the construction of the all-Canadian line. I would also point out that this statement was made some months ago, before the statement had been made about the over-all plan for a Canadian pipe line which embraces

the combined activities of the two companies which were mainly concerned with this problem.
In dealing with this we should all be assured the government has decided definitely that, subject to the availability of financial resources for that purpose, the all-Canadian route will be encouraged, and the encouragement of that route will not be adversely affected by the support of the measure now before us. I do not think we can look at this measure alone without looking at the whole proposal. This is the time for us to decide that not only in the use of gas but in the use of our other natural resources the first consideration in every case will be the development of Canada and the employment of those resources to provide more work for Canadians here in Canada.
There can be no reasonable objection to that proposal by anyone living in the United States. After all, the United States built its great wealth and its great strength upon that basic proposition. They would be the last who could reasonably complain if we adopted the very same policy which was at the root of their rapid and impressive development during those past centuries.
When we have said that let us always make it clear that this does not carry with it any suggestion, such as is sometimes made, that we are refusing to deal on a fair and equitable basis with our friends in the United States. That would be unreasonable; it would be unsound; it would be contrary to the future interests of our country. Nevertheless we must remember that as we encourage immigration we are encouraging new demands for work at a time when there are those who are already looking for work in Canada. It is doubly important that we should remember that everyone who comes to Canada is also looking for a chance to work. It does seem inconsistent to me that we should encourage and accept as new citizens of Canada people who need work, while at the same time we export any resources which could more economically be used here, because the exportation of resources is not merely the export of some physical commodity; it is the export of work itself. As we encourage new working hands to join with us in building the greater Canada of tomorrow, it is surely wise for us to be certain that we keep within Canada whatever sources of employment are required to give work to these new Canadians on their arrival.
This proposal is related, and directly related, to other measures 'which have been before us at different times in the past two .years. Long debates have taken place in
Niagara Gas Transmission Limited this house on pipe lines in the past. Quite frankly, those debates were for the purpose of keeping those bills before this house so the need for a truly all-Canadian policy on this subject should be established. I know that on the other side of the house there was a great deal of resentment that those private measures, which were in fact government bills for all practical purposes, were held so long in this house before being passed. Nevertheless, it is significant that out of those debates there has emerged the Canada-first policy which was advocated by the members of this party. We made it clear that in those extended debates, which it would perhaps not be inappropriate to describe as filibusters, the one purpose was to use the right of debate to insist by every means within the power of the opposition that the interests of Canadians be given first consideration before we agreed to the export of this or other resources from Canada.
The debates on this subject began with the oil pipe line. I have no hesitation in saying that I still regret the decision of the government to support the construction of an oil pipe line south of the great lakes before we were assured of an all-Canadian pipe line. Nevertheless I am not going to renew the debate on that matter. However, I would point out that some of the warnings were justified. That line was constructed to carry oil to Superior, Wisconsin, from which port the oil could be carried by tankers to the Canadian refineries at Sarnia. However, it was only a short time after the oil pipe line to Superior was completed that the next step was taken and the pipe line was extended through the United States south of the great lakes and then back into Canada at Sarnia.
I do not believe for one moment that this intention was not in the minds of those who constructed that pipe line in the first place. I think that intention should have been disclosed to us. I am not making the statement that the government withheld information in their possession, but I am making the statement that I do not believe that those who constructed the pipe line so suddenly changed their minds after it had been constructed to Superior.
However, I agree with the statement that there is a difference between the transmission of oil and the transmission of gas. Gas can be carried only by pipe line; oil can be carried not only by pipe line but by tankers and tank cars. Therefore oil is more easily moved to different places than gas. I think it is certain that unless the gas pipe line is constructed through Canada we will be denied any advantages of the use of that gas in the area through which that pipe line
2724	HOUSE OF
Niagara Gas Transmission Limited would pass, which would not otherwise be served if it were to pass south of the great lakes. I mention this now because I believe it is a consideration in support of my request that the government assure us that in supporting this measure we have the right to do so in the belief that appropriate steps will be taken to make sure that the market developed in the metropolitan area of Toronto as a result of this will be available to the suppliers of Canadian gas when that pipe line is completed in two years, as we hope it will be.
Sometimes this subject is discussed as though you could deal with it only on the basis of dollars and cents in determining the economic factors which should be borne in mind in reaching a decision. Mr. Chairman, the difference in cost, which has been estimated variously to be in the neighbourhood of $25 million, is something which should not be left to stand alone when considering what the effect would be of building this pipe line through Canada the whole way.
If the pipe line were to be built south of the great lakes presumably it would go south at some point near Winnipeg. You would have half of a pipe line costing in the neighbourhood of $300 million being built in the United States. That money would go to workmen in the United States. It would go for the purchase of land in the United States. It would go for supplies in the United States. It must be perfectly obvious to everyone that we would lose a great deal more than $25 million by the route passing into the United States and returning to Canada at some point in eastern Ontario. When I say eastern Ontario I am speaking of the Sarnia area which is in fact eastern Ontario, although it is sometimes called western Ontario.
The advantages of this construction should not be regarded as selfish advantages desired by people living in any particular community; nevertheless let us look at what would happen. If this gas was transmitted by a Canadian route instead of going south of the lakes it would pass through such cities as Kenora, Fort William, Port Arthur, Sault Ste. Marie, Sudbury and North Bay. There would be feeder lines into other areas in northern Ontario. It would then pass on to serve the Toronto area, the Montreal area, southwestern Ontario, eastern Ontario and those parts of Quebec which would receive service from feeder lines. The possible use of gas throughout that area is tremendous. Unless there were diversions of gas from this United States pipe line at different points, there would be nothing to equal the demand that would be 

created by those very active and important communities which would be using gas from this pipe line.
New demands are emerging almost every day. They are dramatic, they are romantic. For example, we have all been reading the dramatic story of the new discovery of metal in the Manitouwadge area in Ontario. Already it is estimated by the Ontario department of mines that there would be a daily demand of ten million cubic feet of gas a day in that area alone, which was nothing but bush only a short time ago. It is estimated also that there would be a demand of ten million cubic feet a day at Cobalt in Ontario and Noranda in Quebec. Similar demands would be expected in these other communities.
The history of the use of power of this kind, whether it be gas, oil or electricity, is that the consumption multiplies far beyond the estimates of the most optimistic at the time the original arrangements are made. I have seen what happened in Ontario in the use of hydroelectric energy. There is no reason to expect other than that the use of natural gas as a source of power for industry as well as for domestic fuel for the home owner will multiply far beyond the original expectations, in the same way as in the case of electricity and oil. That being the case, we may expect that the first use of gas in these areas will create new uses and new demands. All this will be lost, not only to those areas that would have this advantage but to those carrying the gas to eastern Canada, unless that route is followed.
I think this bill is part of what I referred to earlier as a great mosaic of development of a new source of fuel and power in Canada. I hope it will be regarded by the members of this house as part of that mosaic. However, can we have an assurance that it is part of that mosaic, and that in offering support of this measure we do so with the assurance that there is no wavering in the declaration of policy in regard to an allCanadian gas pipe line?
I do not believe it would be right to pass from this discussion now without commending those who so persistently and for so long have fought for this policy. This policy has been stated, and we can say without boasting that this was the policy we advocated from the beginning, and continued to advocate over long weeks and months. I hope we will have the assurance now by the one minister who is in a position to give that assurance that this bill with its two sections does not stand alone. I hope we can have the assurance that the great possibilities in the development of an all-Canadian route, with full consideration for the rights and expectations of

the producers in Alberta as well as the consumers in eastern Canada, will be part and parcel of the decision we make in approving this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I will say at once I believe there is no substantial difference between the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and myself as to what we hope to do in serving Ontario and Quebec with natural gas.
I think, though, I should at once correct one misconception. The Leader of the Opposition asked the government to give assurances that if this bill passed certain things would happen. I would like to point out to him that by an act of this parliament the importation of gas across the international boundary was brought under the provisions of the Pipe Lines Act. Prior to that legislation the government had. no authority whatever to control the importation of gas from the United States, as he knows. The Pipe Lines Act, before it was amended, provided for gas moved across provincial boundaries, but perhaps through an oversight it did not provide for the movement of gas across the international boundary.
However, this is a private member's bill asking for the incorporation of a company to build a pipe line. No import permit is required to do so and if parliament passes this bill the government as such would have no control over the situation. It is true that the bill must go to the board of transport commissioners, which, as hon. members know, is a judicial board. I sincerely hope the board of transport commissioners will be seized with the long-range problem of bringing gas to Ontario and Quebec, and will measure the effect of the application made under this bill with regard to the over-all results.
I would emphasize, however, that once this bill is passed the machinery operates as set out in the Pipe Lines Act, and no further federal government authority of any kind is required. If the board of transport commissioners should decide that no regard should be paid to tne situation brought about by plans to bring gas from western Canada, the government would be powerless to intervene.
Having said that I would point out that I am not opposing the second reading of this bill. I believe that if a responsible company desires to build a pipe line for a purpose which is in the interests of Canada or any section thereof, then the incorporation should be granted. But I believe it is the duty of the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, to which this bill will
Niagara Gas Transmission Limited be referred, to bring the interested parties before it in order to deal with the points raised by the Leader of the Opposition, which are certainly most important, and to report to the house its findings based on what it learns from an examination of the bill. I have no doubt the committee will wish to see the contract for gas which would be implemented through the building of this pipe line, and that it will also wish to make sure that the Toronto area is reserved for natural gas from the west.
The incorporators of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited have embarked on the largest operation of this kind ever undertaken. It is a project which will adequately supply gas to the fuel-starved areas of Ontario and Quebec. In regard to this great national project it is my desire, and I am sure the desire of every hon. member of this house, to see that nothing intervenes in the meantime which would jeopardize the success of that project.
Strangely enough I have never received any communication from the incorporators of this bill. I have read letters addressed to me in advertisements in the press, but I have never had a letter laid on my desk which was signed by anyone connected with the Consumers' Gas Company. I must say I did not read these letters very carefully because I do not care to be addressed through the public press, but it seems to me an extraordinary complex must exist in certain sections of Ontario, when people prefer to address a minister of the crown in that fashion. However, I do not resent that particularly. I merely wish to emphasize that I know very little about the plans of the incorporators of this bill.

Mr. Chairman, a few weeks ago I had the privilege of telling the house that the present legislation involved a fair and middle of the road course. The legislation has now come back from the banking and commerce committee and I still am of the same opinion. But at the same time I think it is my privilege and my duty to draw the attention of the house to certain recommendations I made at that time which for some reason the banking and commerce committee has not seen fit to adopt. I refer to the scope of the National Housing Act. I think the act in itself is national in scope, but it should also be national in its application.
When speaking early in January I suggested that the down payment should be uniform at 10 per cent for all categories of houses, not only for housing costing $8,000.
I merely made a simple statement at that time, but today I should like to amplify it and give the house the reasons which led me to make this recommendation. During the debate an hon. member from the province of Quebec asked that loans should be made for the benefit of the large families of Quebec.
I should like to correct this statement, because I do not believe Quebec is the only province in Canada that has large families. I do not believe large families are only a matter of creed, religion or race. I can cite from history, for example, the case of George III and Queen Charlotte. They had 15 children. So I say that under the housing act we should as far as possible give everybody the privilege of borrowing the amount of money they need to build a home that will suit their own purposes.
A man with three children will need a greater loan than $8,000, because if he does build a home worth $8,000 he is building a slum house. I regret that the banking and commerce committee has not seen fit to take this fact into consideration. We speak of immigration and enlarging our population, but I think we should take care of our human capital at home because our human capital is most vital and important. I have no objection to bringing immigrants to this


country; they can become very good Canadian citizens. But at the same time I think we should see that our Canadian families have the possibility of expanding. I think we should let nature take its course. That may seem a humorous remark to the house, nevertheless I think it has a social bearing. I believe it is my duty to again draw the attention of the house to this matter.
In the second place, I wish to state that there is also an economic reason. If we grant loans on houses and give preference to $8,000 homes, we are creating a market for $8,000 homes. If we build too many $8,000 homes under present circumstances the housing market in Canada will not have the diversity which is needed in any commercial market. I do not think a manufacturer who produced only size eight stockings or gave preference to that size just because he had machinery for that size of stocking would be able to compete in the market. This same argument applies in the housing field.
I should like to make a few remarks on the application of the National Housing Act. I said in January I was glad to see this bill before the house because I believed it would solve the problem of housing where the old act failed. I can say now, and I shall repeat it in this house, that the old act failed in my constituency to the extent of about 80 per cent of the population. Why was that so? It was simply because the joint loans which were made through the finance companies were left entirely in the hands of the finance companies. If they did not wish to lend in one community or another, then those communities were denied the benefits of the act.
Under the new bill, and I must bring this to the attention of the house, the people of Canada will ultimately be footing the bill if foreclosures occur. For this reason, I feel that we should give every Canadian and every region in this country the opportunity to get loans. In the international field this country has seen fit to give grants under the Colombo plan. Well, I agree with that. On the other hand, I do not feel there should be any underprivileged regions in Canada. I should like, therefore, to see this act applied in such a way that all regions are given a fair chance to get loans. If the act is applied properly by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and if the lending institutions refuse loans in certain regions, then I advocate that the government step in and say that loans must be made in every town in this country. Then we would have a National Housing Act applied nationally. That is what I am asking here tonight. I should like to see fair play for all Canadians.

After all, the principle of no taxation without representation does not And its full expression merely because a constituency has a member sitting in this house. It finds its full expression through the benefits which the whole population derive from that taxation. If the people of Canada as a whole are going to foot the bill in case of foreclosures, they should be given an opportunity of obtaining loans under this National Housing Act. There should be no underprivileged regions.
In closing, I recommend that these few remarks be taken into consideration, and I thank the government for whatever steps are taken to see that all the people get a fair chance to get loans under this act.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I was rather interested in the remarks of the hon. member who just took his seat. I feel that he expressed some of the doubts which many of us have about the bill which is before us. I should like to invite him, a little later, to vote against the bill, as no doubt I shall.
The main purpose of this legislation, as I understand it, is to try to find a method of easing Canada's housing shortage.	Some
weeks ago, along with the hon. member for Nanaimo, I voted against the motion for second reading of this bill. I did so because I was convinced that it was not an effective answer to our housing difficulties.	After
sitting in the banking and commerce committee during a substantial number of meetings I am even more convinced of that fact today.
What is the housing situation in Canada at the moment? I think all hon. members would agree there is a very heavy backlog of housing because of the depression and the war years. As a matter of fact, the housing shortage continues to be desperately acute. Mr. Mansur, the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation summed it up in one sentence, in this way. He said, at page 88 of the committee evidence, that "starting from 1948, I think the effective demand is higher today than at any other time". We, as members, I suppose must assume that this legislation is the government's answer to that present demand.
Surely in evaluating this bill tonight, whether we sit on the government or on the opposition side, we should ask ourselves one question. Will this legislation ease the acute housing shortage in Canada? Will this bill give housing to the people who need it? It seems to me there are a number of weaknesses in the legislation which could make it virtually ineffective. I hope this will not prove to be the case, but I fear it will.
National Housing Act
In the first place, so far as I can see this bill will do nothing to provide housing for those in the lower income groups. Mr. Mansur placed some very interesting evidence before the committee at page 161 of the proceedings. He put on the record several tables. The first table shows that to build a $10,000 house and amortize it over a 20-year period with interest at 5-5 per cent, a man must have an income of $4,002. If we look at the figures which the Department of National Revenue puts out, in its report "Taxation statistics for 1952", we find that 85-4 per cent of Canadian wage earners in that year did not earn $4,000. In other words, if we do not count the income of wives only 15 per cent of Canadian wage earners could qualify under this act to build a $10,000 house.
If we take a $12,000 house-and many people with children would have to build a $12,000 house with the extra bedrooms- we find that Mr. Mansur's statement shows that with interest at 5-5 per cent a person must have an income of $4,686. In the year I mentioned, 90 per cent of Canadian wage earners did not earn that amount. I suggest, therefore, that only 10 per cent of Canadian wage earners could qualify to build a $12,000 home under those circumstances. Thus, as I see it, the first weakness in this legislation is that it will do nothing to bring home ownership to the vast working class that really needs it.
In the second place, if I interpret this legislation correctly we have no assurance that even if the bill passes, the mortgage funds available for housing will increase. It was pointed out this afternoon that as soon as this bill passes the government will cease making joint loans. Thus there will be approximately $60 millon which was available last year from this source that will not be available this year. In other words, in this bill the government is abandoning what little responsibility it did have in the field of house financing. Mr. Mansur pointed out fairly clearly, as did Mr. Bryden of the insurance companies, that in the coming year Canadian insurance companies will have smaller amounts of mortgage funds available for housing than they had in past years. Therefore this legislation is designed, I suppose, to more or less take up the slack, to make bank deposits available for long-term housing loans. Mr. Speaker, we should realize that this is only permissive legislation. We have no assurance that the banks will make available the amount of money we need for adequate housing.
In his evidence Mr. Atkinson, vice-president and general manager of the Royal Bank made it very clear that the banks did not

National Housing Act
regard housing as a suitable field for investment. Time and again the banks have told us that they are already fully "loaned" and that they have not large sums available for housing mortgages. Thus I say this legislation gives no assurance that the banks will lend the amount of mortgage money required. It is very clear that the banks themselves are dubious about this legislation.
In the third place, I suggest that this bill will do nothing to provide cheaper houses. Certainly in my constituency, and I presume in others, one of the main obstacles to a man becoming the owner of a house is the very high cost. Under this new plan housing is going to be much more expensive than it was under the old plan. Under the new plan, for instance, the purchaser must pay a premium for insuring the loan. That will amount to 2 per cent of the mortgage. If the mortgage is $10,000 that amount will be approximately $200. Moreover, the lower down payment, the extended amortization period and the higher housing interest rate are going to force the prospective owner to pay more for his house in the long run.
I should like to compare the cost of the same house built under the old plan and the new plan. For example, let us take a $10,000 house. Under the old plan the down payment was 20 per cent, the interest rate 5J per cent, and the amortization period 20 years. Under the old plan the total cost was $2,000 down, $8,000 principal, $4,878 interest. Under the new plan the down payment will be $1,000; the interest rate at least 5J per cent-it may be 5f per cent; we have not been told yet-the amortization period 25 years. The total cost could be $1,000 down; $9,000 principal; $7,482 interest. I have compounded the interest semi-annually in both cases. In other words, an identical house built under the new plan is going to cost the purchaser, by the time he owns the title, roughly $2,600 more than it would cost him under the old plan. I suggest that is not a very satisfactory answer to the nation's housing needs.
There is one other aspect of this bill which I do not like. Even if the banks can find adequate funds, they may do so only by taking those funds from somewhere else. Such a diversion might make it more difficult for farmers in eastern and western Canada to obtain funds from the banks at a time when they need them urgently. The banks might also be forced to tighten up on industrial and commercial loans. In other words, I maintain that this legislation is not the answer to Canada's housing problem.
Even if the bill passes new houses will still be beyond the reach of the average Canadian family. Under this legislation the

interest rate is excessive, the over-all costs are too high, and the income qualifications are too severe. In my opinion this legislation is little more than a mirage to the vast majority of would-be house owners.

Under this legislation the government is passing the housing buck to Canadian banks, and the banks understandably are reluctant to receive it. They are not enthused about being made the goat. The bill is unsatisfactory and inadequate, and I shall continue to vote against it at every stage, if further votes are called. We in the C.C.F. still believe that the present housing problem in Canada can only be solved by the marshalling of public funds to complement private construction.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the evidence heard during the sittings of the banking and
commerce committee has not only been very interesting but it has enabled us to appreciate the great service rendered by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to the Canadian people.
The associations that have been called upon to do business with the corporation have been pleased to recognize that they have always obtained useful and frank co-operation from the corporation.
There is no doubt that the benefits of the new legislation will be appreciated by citizens in a position to take advantage of them, that is, people earning $3,600 and over per year. I am in favour of the present bill because it is absolutely necessary in spite of its shortcomings. I would like however to call the hon. minister's attention to the need of helping family heads earning less than $3,000 per year. In that connection it might be advantageous to copy the Quebec family housing act and grant a rebate of interest to the borrower.
The housing problem is a highly social matter and, in my opinion, those who are less fortunate should be looked after first, because they are the ones most in need of help and protection. To save a few hundred dollars, most workers must toil and make sacrifices for several years. It is practically impossible for them to meet the conditions prescribed by the present legislation.
In my constituency, particularly in the city of Chicoutimi and the town of Port Alfred, farsighted and courageous men, moved by an extraordinary civic spirit, have succeeded, through hard work, will power, steadfastness and in spite of many obstacles, in organizing housing co-operatives, the results of which

are now the pride and beauty of those towns. It is the duty of the government to stimulate that kind of activity and to contribute to its development.

speechtext:
In the first place it must be said that it is rather regrettable the government saw fit to bring this bill back to the house before the minutes of the final meeting of the banking and commerce committee on the bill were made available to all hon. members. However, in the minutes that hon. members now have in their possession we have perhaps a basis for discussing the actual realities with regard to this bill.
I have always regretted that I was out of the house at the time the Minister of Public Works made his speech with regard to the criticisms of this bill by members of the opposition. Of course since that time I have had an opportunity of reading his speech, and I must congratulate him upon it. But I wonder if before he and his officials see this bill put into effect he will think he was quite wise in the view he took on that occasion of the position taken by the members of the opposition.
I have in mind, for instance, the criticism he made of the various estimates made by hon. members with regard to the possibility of people with lower average incomes owning their homes under this bill. Referring to the remarks of the hon. member for Broadview, he said it was a complete distortion of the realities of the situation to suggest that only houses of $10,000 and up could be built under this bill. The minister is reported at page 1574 of Hansard of January 28 as follows:
I have just checked with Central Mortgage, who tell me that in 1953 approximately 25 per cent of the houses for home ownership were below $10,000 in cost. He took the example of a $10,000 house, and gave the impression that anybody with an income of less than $3,860 a year need not apply for a loan under the National Housing Act.
I think the hon. member for Broadview was probably on fairly sound ground when he took that position. We find on page 163 of the minutes of the banking and commerce committee a table set out which was presented to the committee by Central Mortgage showing the relationship between home ownership income and down payment and interest rates. I notice, curiously enough, that the example Central Mortgage and Housing saw fit to present to the banking
National Housing Act
and commerce committee was that of a $10,000 house. While it may be true, as the minister says, that in 1953 a number of houses were built at a cost of less than $10,000, he does not tell us how much less than $10,000.
When we turn to a statement presented to the committee by Mr. Bryden, appearing at page 170 of the evidence, we find set out the experience of the companies for which he was speaking. He had some interesting figures to give. He showed that in 1953, which was only last year, the average loan for new single houses was $7,990. If it had been $10 more the average house cost would have been $10,000 in 1953. It is quite true that because the average was $7,990 for an 80 per cent loan instead of $8,000 there were a number of houses built at a cost of less than $10,000. But how much less? How important a factor in the whole picture did they constitute?
As I say, I was interested in the minister's tour de force on the second reading of this bill, but I was interested also in what he had to say at an earlier stage. At that time he was more in the role of a statesman introducing legislation than a politician replying to attacks in the House of Commons. As I recollect it, the minister was telling us at that time of the manner in which the government through this legislation was enabling larger sums to be made available for mortgage purposes for the building of houses. Then, so that the banks would not endanger the liquidity of their assets, he pointed out that there were two features in the bill which offset the possibly dangerous tendency involved in this new departure in banking practice.
These two new features were, first, the fact that mortgages issued under the authority of this legislation would have a comparable status with government bonds for the purpose of deposit with the Bank of Canada for loans. The other was the insurance feature whereby when a bank had finally evicted a delinquent borrower they could go to Central Mortgage and Housing and they would bail them out.
We had before the banking and commerce committee Mr. Atkinson, who is general manager of the Royal Bank of Canada. He had a few things to tell us. He was asked a question with regard to this strange proposition of the minister that these loans being made available for deposit with the Bank of Canada ensured the liquidity of the bank's assets. In answering that question Mr. Atkinson apparently was of a different frame of mind from the minister.

speechtext: It was an effort to reduce the amount of the down payment on houses generally which everybody in this house has seemed very anxious to do.
