That is one of the things I pointed out on various occasions. It is one of the penalties a borrower must pay if he wants a lower down payment. It does, at the same time, widen the band of potential home owners, and I think that is a good thing. This, therefore, was an effort to reduce the down payment and at the same time make available the greatest amount of loans for low cost houses.

Clause agreed to.
Clause 8 agreed to.
On clause 9-Payment by corporation upon conveyance of property.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
On clause 9 I should like to observe that the fact there are very few points being raised with respect to the clauses of the bill is, I think, a tribute to the thoroughness with which the banking and commerce committee reviewed these clauses in detail.
There was a point, however, discussed with the minister concerning the form of clause

9, subclause (d). This clause was rewritten by one of the technical amendments introduced into the bill in committee. There is no problem about the intent with respect to the compounding of interest in case of default, but there was a serious question raised as to whether the clause, in the revised form in which it appears now in the reprint of the bill, does carry out that intent. I offered an amendment with a view to eliminating what appeared to be a difference of opinion as to whether the clause, as reprinted and amended, did give effect to the intent.
The problem arises, Mr. Chairman, in clause 9(d) (i) with respect to the meaning of the words, "for the period of such excess." The question was whether the use of the words "of such excess" limits the application of the compounding to the period following the conclusion of the first six months of default. Three lines above those words you find the expression "in excess of six months", and *with the use of the expression "period of such excess" it does suggest that a proper interpretation of the section means that the compounding applies only to that portion of the arrears arising at the end of the six months, and not to the portion of arrears accruing during the first six months of the period of default.
The view expressed by Mr. Mansur in the committee was that there was no problem on the interpretation, and that the compounding will be applied in the usual manner to all arrears dating from the date of the first monthly default. Perhaps the minister is prepared to make a statement on the view taken with respect to the meaning of the expression.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am aware there has been some question of the adequacy of the wording, but at the same time I agree with the hon. member for Eglinton that there is no question whatever as to the intention. This particular subsection was discussed at great length by the committee, and then by various individuals on the committee. I have had discussions on the same point with Mr. Fortin, who is representing the Dominion Mortgage and Investments Association, and I know his views on it as well.
It seems to be one of those points in which lawyers regard various combinations of words as expressing different meanings. After discussing this both with the law officers of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and with the Department of Justice I am advised that the words as now set forth in the clause in the bill are adequate. The law officers of the crown are satisfied that the clause is so worded that the approved lender will receive interest at the appropriate
National Housing Act
rates compounded in accordance with normal mortgage practice at the six months rest periods, for the full period of eighteen months, if the default period extends to this length. It is the intention of the government that this should be the case.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I was on my
feet, Mr. Chairman, to raise a point on clause 8 when you rushed through 8 to clause 9 and then called on the hon. member for Eglinton on clause 9. May I revert to clause 8?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: Is it agreed that the hon. member has permission to revert to clause 8?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: Agreed.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: This clause refers to co-operative housing associations. I wonder whether the minister can clarify the situation for us. He will recall that it was discussed at the final meeting of the committee, and that is one of the reasons I regret the minutes of that meeting are not here. I rather gathered from what communication I have had that there was some misunderstanding as to the position of the minister and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation concerning this proposition. It will be recalled that a question was asked as to whether a cooperative housing association could qualify as a low rental housing project, and with some qualifications I gathered that it could do so. One qualification was that there was no technical assumption of title, and that provision could be made for the member of such an association who moved out of the low income bracket to receive his equity in order to make it available to someone still in that bracket. Could the minister give us some clarification of that position?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman, this clause was discussed by the committee on the last day of the sittings, at which time I made a statement which I thought clarified the position. I said that although it was not the intention to set up a separate class of home owners who could qualify for the low rate of interest normally applying to the limited dividend section, if a co-operative could in fact qualify as a limited dividend company then it would be eligible for the low rate of interest prevailing for limited dividend operations.
There is one requirement in respect to co-operatives as set forth in clause 16 of this bill. There must be independent management of the co-operative, and that is one of the points we have been discussing with the Co-operative Union. I had quite a discussion

National Housing Act
with Mr. Staples, the president of the Cooperative Union, this evening, and I believe he understands our position on the matter.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: Clause 9 contains a provision calling for the payment to the approved lender of an acquisition fee of $125. It does not seem clear how that figure is arrived at. Is it a flat amount, or is it only an estimate in order to cover all exigencies, or is it a maximum figure? Suppose, for example, the acquisition costs fall below $125. In some cases they may not amount to anything. Would the approved lender still get $125, regardless of what his costs might be?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, he would.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: If that is so we should have some explanation of why the provision is there, because eventually it is going to come out of the taxpayers of Canada. What is the reason for guaranteeing $125 as an acquisition fee, even though the cost to the approved lender may be considerably less? If it read "not exceeding $125" we would have some protection; otherwise we have none.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: This figure was evolved as the result of many conversations between the lending institutions and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. There is no doubt that the average cost of getting title to a property is considerably in excess of $125. The lending institutions think this is far too little, especially if they are obliged to go through legal proceedings. There are some instances in which one would hope and expect that they would get quit claims, and then their charges would not be as great as $125. We took this as a minimum average, having regard to conditions across the country. The lending institutions believe that their average costs are more likely to be $225 than $125.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
That refers
only to the expenses of the lending institutions if they have to go to law. What about the poor home owner who may have to go to law against the mortgage companies? Does he get any compensation? It has happened before now.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: There is no provision in the legislation for that. That does not happen very often.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: Would the Minister of Public Works care to make a statement relative to the period allowed for a loan to be in default? Is there any definite period allowed for that sort of thing, or is it left to the discretion of the bank?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: Under the provisions of the legislation the lending institutions must report to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation if a loan is in default for a period of three months, as to principal, interest and taxes. Then it will be a matter for decision as to what action will be taken. There is a period of 18 months provided in the legislation, during which time they are required to get clear title to the property.

Clause agreed to.
Clause 10 agreed to.
On clause 11-Investments by corporations.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: I presume this is the clause under which the government would act if it does intend to carry out such a policy as I suggested earlier this afternoon. Can the minister give us any information as to the government's real intention? Does it intend to take off the hands of the chartered banks the mortgages they have issued and assume the role of the lender, or to take them off their hands and assume the task of disposing of these mortgages otherwise? We should know what is the government's real purpose in this regard.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: As I said in my second speech, which the hon. member for Nanaimo termed statesmanlike, before I became a politician-

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: He is a new member.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: You will never do that again.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I said that our considerations were for the liquidity, negotiability and marketability of these mortgage documents, and we had in mind the general structure and the healthy structure of the Canadian banking system. My hon. friend made certain comments on my references to liquidity, but I would remind him that we were concerned with the broader concept. He was concerned only with the ability of the banks to borrow from the central bank whereas we, as a government, must of course be concerned with the matter of general public confidence in the banking system.
It is the hope that the banks themselves will be able to operate and provide the amount of loan money necessary for operations under this legislation and to ensure a high house building program in Canada. To the extent that the banks, for one reason or another, in the light of developing circumstances wish to use insured mortgages to obtain money from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, they may proceed under clause 11 (a) and (b) which are the enabling sections to provide the necessary

authority to Central Mortgage to buy insured mortgages or to lend on the security of insured mortgages as required.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: I am sorry that in answering this question the minister decided to take as his model his second speech rather than his statesmanlike speech. I still do not know, and I suggest no hon. member knows, what the government really has in mind with regard to this clause. We are entitled to know in view of this fact. The banks told us before the banking and commerce committee that in the first place it is an illusion to imagine they have any large pool of available capital. In the second place, Mr. Atkinson told us that the only way the banks could possibly participate to any appreciable extent in this scheme would be if a market was developed for mortgage funds. I suggest that here there is a suggestion that the government itself is going to provide that market, and I think we are entitled to know the government's fiscal and monetary mechanisms by which they may do so.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: I do recall that when Mr. Towers gave evidence before the committee he said the banks should have no difficulty in making loans of $100 million a year under this legislation. I would imagine that it was in his mind that such could be done without difficulty at all, and that a larger amount could easily be envisaged.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: He said it would not be a large sum for the banks.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: May I have a word in regard to this section, because the minister referred to it while he was speaking this afternoon. He wanted to know if I recalled clause 11. What I was speaking of this afternoon was the possibility of the banks carrying out this housing scheme by creating more credit, and the minister suggested to me that under this section they would be able to do that. Under this section they would not be able to do it. It is true that under this section the corporation can buy back mortgages from the banks, but that would only be reimbursing them for the money they had already paid out; it would not in any way increase their cash reserves so they would be able to lend new money for the building of houses.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 12-Regulations by governor in council.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Can the minister make any statement as to whether any change is to
National Housing Act
be made in the regulation which determines the minimum income that a person can have and still qualify for an N.H.A. loan?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: I take it that the hon. member is referring to the 23 per cent which is normally considered to be the limit for good credit risk. If a borrower must devote more than 23 per cent of his income to the payment for his home he normally goes beyond that category. The only stipulation set forth in the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation regulation is that when the ratio gets beyond 23 per cent the loan must be discussed by the lending institution with Central Mortgage. Up to that time the lending institution is free to act without consulting Central Mortgage as to the risk involved. There are loans made beyond the 23 per cent, depending on the circumstances, but the 23 per cent is the point at which under the regulations there must be discussions between the corporation and the lending institution.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: Does the minister say that has been the case under the act as it has stood, or is that the situation envisaged at the moment?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: That has been the case. I am informed that in 27 per cent of the loans made in 1953 the ratio was greater than 23 per cent.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: When a person seeks a loan where the amount to be paid would be in excess of 23 per cent of his income, who initiates discussions with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the applicant for the loan or the money-lender?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: The lending institution.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: Suppose a lending institution is not prepared to initiate those discussions; has the applicant for a loan any recourse?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: They are the ones who take the mortgage risk. Application is made to the lending institution, and that is the normal channel.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: My question is still valid. Has the applicant any recourse or appeal? The minister indicated that the ceiling is 23 per cent of one's income. As he knows, there are many people who have to pay an even greater percentage of their income by way of rent. It seems to me that there ought to be some way for such persons, when the lending institution turns them down, to make an appeal to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Is there not some way in which that can be done?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not understand how one could force a lending institution to lend money on a risk they did not consider to be

National Housing Act
good. I think that is the criterion. We are trying by these means to enable the lending institutions to lend money to encourage the production of new houses in Canada. The negotiation is between the lending institution and the borrower. The government extends its facilities to enable the lending institutions to lend money more expeditiously.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: Do I take it that despite all that has been said in the house, in the press, in the committee and in other places about this matter, for all practical purposes it still stands that nobody whose income is less than around $3,800 a year can qualify for an N.H.A. loan? If that is the case there has certainly been very little improvement.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: I would point out to the hon. member that in Ottawa last year more than one-quarter of the loans made under this legislation were in that category.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: Does the minister or the hon. member for Ottawa West know what the situation is in other parts of the country? What is it that puts Ottawa in that special category?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: I do not think it is a special category. That is the normal practice, for the lending companies to send in the applications and have them considered.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: May I point out that in Toronto about 17 per cent of the loans were in that category.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: It is good to have these parliamentary assistants to the minister giving us information. Perhaps somebody else can tell us what the picture is in other cities, and also for the country as a whole.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member can give it for Winnipeg.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: I do not know. I am not a parliamentary assistant to the minister.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
In his speech the minister
referred to the creditworthiness of a borrower, and I am just wondering whether a person who qualifies under this 23 per cent would be considered as a creditworthy borrower.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: I do not think we can take that as a criterion. It is a matter of the lending institution determining the creditworthiness of a borrower. A man might have only 20 per cent and still have a bad credit rating, and the lending institution would not accept his mortgage loan. As I said before, the 23 per cent is simply the point at which the lending institution comes to Central Mortgage and says, "Let us discuss this and see whether we should make a loan".

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: The minister says that the lending institution comes to Central Mortgage, but that is done only if the lending institution decides to follow that course. So far as the individual applicant is concerned, if the lending institution says "No," I gather that he would have no recourse. I think there will be considerable disappointment that there has been no improvement in connection with this very important point over which there has been so much discussion while this matter has been before us.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there is some information I should like to have. I hope the minister will forgive me, as I was not a member of the committee and the information I want may have been supplied already. It occurs to me that there may be cases where the credit of the borrower is good. He may want to borrow perhaps only 75 per cent of the cost of his house, or even a smaller percentage. Is it possible that he would be informed by Central Mortgage and Housing that the lending value of his house was far below the cost and he could not be granted a loan even though he himself was considered to be a good risk? I would like to know how the lending value of a property is arrived at. Is there an element of speculation as to what the future value may be? In other words, if you have identical houses in different places would the lending value be the same? Is there some formula by which the lending value is arrived at, so that a borrower could be informed beforehand and have an idea whether it would be possible for him to build in a certain area?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: Generally speaking the lending value is based on current construction costs in the area plus a 5 per cent profit. That was explained in committee. I know the hon. member was not a member of the committee, and I am pleased to have the opportunity of explaining that to him. As regards the question whether a loan could be less than the maximum prescribed under the act, the answer is that it could go down to 70 per cent of the appraised lending value of the house.

Clause agreed to.
Clauses 13 to 16 inclusive agreed to.
On clause 17-Loans to borrowers engaged in mining, lumbering, logging, or fishing.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on clause 17, the function of which is to make loans available to operators in the mining, lumbering, logging and fishing industries, I would like to ask the minister if he would outline the considerations in committee which led to the elimination of the agricultural industry

from this particular clause. I know consideration was given to this matter in the banking and commerce committee, but the elimination is so striking that I feel some additional clarification would be helpful.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, knowing the hon. member's interest in the farming community I am very glad to be able to inform him that there is a provision for financing homes on farms under part I of the act. As to why farming was not mentioned in this particular clause, there are three reasons which occur to me, though there are perhaps others. In the first place the parent company must be an incorporated entity, and there are not many large corporations which are primarily concerned with the farming industry. Second, loans have to be secured on mortgages on the land on which the houses are to be built, and this sometimes presents difficulties because of the fact that there is often a mortgage on the land for other purposes. Third, the period of amortization has to be 15 years, and this might not be appropriate for farming purposes.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: While I do not wish to provoke a discussion on the subject I would suggest that the reasons advanced by the minister as to why agriculture could not be included under clause 17 do not apply in the case of quite a number of ranching concerns in British Columbia. I would like to know whether these concerns would be covered under the other provision he mentioned in part I. The ones I have in mind are practically all incorporated companies which have a considerable problem in providing housing for their employees, even though they own the land.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: The answer is yes.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: They would be covered under that other provision?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: I would like to pursue that statement the minister made regarding mortgages on farm property. In towns you have nothing but the ground on which the house stands; and even supposing a farm was mortgaged, that should not prevent them from obtaining assistance of this kind.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is a
section under part I of the bill which covers that. I am simply saying here that clause 17 applies to incorporated companies, and there are not many farms of the type my hon. friend has in mind which are incorporated companies.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: Can the minister tell us how much activity there has been under the home improvement loans section and how much there is likely to be under the new act?

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have heard over and over again in this committee of the whole the contention that nothing has been done under this act for people with incomes of less than $3,800. That, of course, is absolute nonsense, because one of the most important clauses in this bill has been carried over from the old act, and it provides very large sums of money indeed for the financing of low rental housing projects to be carried out between the federal government and the various provinces. Hon. members opposite who have emphasized with some vigour the necessity for large scale public works have an opportunity right in their own provinces and in their own municipalities to go ahead without further ado and promote such projects. We have the evidence of Dr. Forsey in support of this who said, speaking before the banking and commerce committee, as reported at page 338 of the evidence:

National Housing Act
The subsidized low-rental housing provisions of the present act have not been used as widely as they should have been. This is partly the fault of the municipalities, which have to set the whole thing in motion; partly the fault of citizens who ought to have prodded the municipalities into action; partly the fault of the dominion government, which has been content to hide this particular light under a bushel, instead of setting it on a national candlestick. The government ought to have trumpeted its achievements in putting this section on the statute book four years ago, and ought to have encouraged people all over the country to take advantage of it. Instead, it has been strangely reticent about one of the things it should have been proudest of.
Therefore, if that strong contingent from Saskatchewan wishes to get money for low rental housing projects all it has to do is get busy. The hon. member for Bow River talked a great deal about the wonderful revolving fund in Alberta. All he has to do to get the merry-go-round going around is to get busy and get hold of some of this $50 million.
